q: You arrive on scene, BSI precautions are taken, and the scene is confirmed safe. What is the correct next step in the primary assessment?
options: Ask about the patient's current medications
Obtain a full set of vital signs
Auscultate lung sounds bilaterally
Form a general impression of the patient

q: According to the NREMT Patient Assessment skill sheet, when should systematic bilateral lung auscultation be performed?
options: During the primary assessment, immediately after opening the airway
During the secondary assessment
Only if the patient is unresponsive
During scene size-up, before patient contact

q: A patient doesn't respond to your voice, but withdraws his arm when you apply a painful stimulus to his nail bed. What is his AVPU status?
options: Pain
Unresponsive
Alert
Verbal

q: In the SAMPLE history mnemonic, what does the "M" stand for?
options: Mental status
Medical history
Mechanism of injury
Medications

q: A patient has an isolated ankle injury with no other apparent trauma, a normal mental status, and no significant mechanism of injury. What secondary assessment approach is most appropriate?
options: No secondary assessment is needed
Focused assessment of the injured area
A detailed head-to-toe exam, but only if the patient becomes unconscious
Rapid full-body trauma assessment

q: Which of the following is NOT one of the components of scene size-up?
options: Obtaining a SAMPLE history
BSI/standard precautions
Determining mechanism of injury/nature of illness
Scene safety

q: During scene size-up, why is determining the number of patients important before beginning patient care?
options: It helps decide if additional resources are needed early
It mainly helps the crew decide who documents the run report
It mainly determines which hospital the patient will be transported to
It's primarily used for accurate documentation and billing after the call

q: A patient's "general impression," formed at the start of the primary assessment, is based primarily on:
options: Age, sex, level of distress, and any obvious life threats visible on approach
Laboratory findings obtained after arrival at the hospital
The full set of vital signs obtained after the primary assessment is complete
The detailed SAMPLE history gathered later in the secondary assessment

q: The "chief complaint" refers to:
options: The EMT's own clinical impression of the patient's most serious problem
The mechanism of injury that caused the patient's condition
The specific reason, in the patient's own words, that they called for help
The full set of vital signs recorded at the time of arrival

q: The OPQRST mnemonic is primarily used to:
options: Assess a patient's pain or chief complaint in detail
Guide airway management decisions during resuscitation
Determine scene safety before making patient contact
Calculate a Glasgow Coma Scale score for mental status

q: How often should reassessment generally be performed on an unstable patient during transport?
options: Every 15 minutes
Only once, at the start of transport
Every 5 minutes
Only if the patient requests it

q: A detailed physical exam (a more thorough head-to-toe exam performed after the rapid trauma or focused assessment) is typically performed:
options: Before scene size-up, prior to confirming the scene is safe
En route to the hospital, time and condition permitting
Instead of the primary assessment, skipping the ABCs entirely
Only on patients who explicitly refuse all further care

q: Which finding would most likely make a trauma patient a "load and go" (immediate transport) priority?
options: A minor laceration with controlled bleeding
A patient requesting to walk to the ambulance
Altered mental status with signs of poor perfusion
An isolated, closed forearm fracture with a normal mental status

q: When assessing a patient who is deaf or hard of hearing, which approach is most appropriate?
options: Face the patient, ask their preferred communication method, and use written notes or an interpreter if needed
Speak loudly and slowly, since that's usually easiest for hearing-impaired patients to understand
Communicate mainly through a family member instead of the patient directly
Assume the patient cannot understand any spoken or written language at all

q: Which scenario would most clearly call for eye protection in addition to gloves?
options: Taking a routine blood pressure on a calm, fully cooperative patient
Interviewing a stable patient about their medical history from a safe distance
Applying a simple bandage to a dry, already-closed wound
A patient who is actively vomiting or has arterial bleeding with potential for splashing

q: A conscious patient is breathing adequately but has an SpO2 of 88% with no signs of inadequate ventilation. What's the appropriate oxygen delivery method?
options: Bag-valve mask at 10–12 breaths/min
Nasal cannula at 2 LPM
No supplemental oxygen is needed
Non-rebreather mask at 15 LPM

q: Which finding indicates a patient needs assisted ventilation with a BVM, rather than just supplemental oxygen?
options: Mild wheezing with a rate of 20
A productive cough with a normal respiratory rate
Respiratory rate of 18 with good tidal volume
Respiratory rate of 6 with shallow, irregular breaths

q: When ventilating an apneic adult patient with a BVM and no advanced airway in place, what is the correct ventilation rate?
options: 1 breath every 3–5 seconds (12–20/min)
As fast as possible until color improves
1 breath every 10 seconds (about 6/min)
1 breath every 6 seconds (about 10/min)

q: Which finding in a patient with respiratory distress is the strongest indicator of impending respiratory failure?
options: A respiratory rate of 22 with normal depth and no distress
Diminished or absent breath sounds with visible fatigue
Loud wheezing heard on auscultation throughout both lung fields
Mild nasal flaring with an otherwise normal respiratory effort

q: What's true about cherry-red skin as a sign of carbon monoxide poisoning?
options: It's more common in mild poisoning than in severe, life-threatening poisoning
It appears immediately upon exposure, before any other symptoms
It's an unreliable, often late sign that shouldn't be relied on to rule CO poisoning in or out
It's present in the vast majority of cases and is diagnostic on its own

q: For a conscious adult with a severe (complete) airway obstruction, the recommended intervention is:
options: Back blows only, repeated forcefully as many times as needed, without ever escalating to abdominal or chest thrusts
Abdominal thrusts (or chest thrusts if pregnant/obese) until the obstruction clears or the patient becomes unresponsive
Have the patient lie down flat and wait for the obstruction to dislodge on its own
Immediate needle cricothyrotomy performed in the field on your own judgment, without medical direction or online authorization

q: A patient who is coughing forcefully and can still speak has:
options: A partial airway obstruction with adequate air exchange; encourage continued coughing
A complete airway obstruction requiring immediate abdominal thrusts
No airway involvement at all, since coughing indicates a fully clear airway
A partial obstruction that requires immediate abdominal thrusts to fully clear it

q: An oropharyngeal airway (OPA) should generally NOT be used in which patient?
options: An apneic patient being actively ventilated with a bag-valve mask
An unresponsive patient with no gag reflex and no spontaneous breathing
A patient in cardiac arrest with ongoing chest compressions
A patient who is unresponsive but still has an intact gag reflex

q: Which of the following is a relative contraindication for inserting a nasopharyngeal airway (NPA)?
options: An unresponsive patient with no facial trauma
A patient who is apneic and needs immediate ventilation
A patient with an intact gag reflex but no other injuries
Suspected severe facial or skull fracture

q: When suctioning an adult patient's airway, how long should a single suction attempt generally be limited to?
options: There is no time limit
No more than about 15 seconds
Up to 60 seconds continuously
Suction should be continued until all secretions are completely cleared, however long that takes

q: When ventilating a patient with a BVM, what is the best indicator that ventilations are effective?
options: The bag feels completely empty after every squeeze
Loud gurgling sounds during ventilation
Visible, adequate chest rise with each breath
The patient's color does not matter as long as the bag is being squeezed

q: A conscious patient in respiratory distress from a suspected asthma exacerbation will typically be most comfortable in which position?
options: Sitting upright or leaning forward (tripod position)
Trendelenburg position, with the head lower than the feet
Left lateral recumbent, lying on the left side
Supine, flat on the back with legs elevated

q: Which condition can cause a falsely normal or elevated pulse oximetry reading despite the patient actually being hypoxic?
options: A simple nosebleed with no other symptoms
A twisted ankle with localized swelling
Carbon monoxide poisoning
Mild anxiety with a normal breathing pattern

q: A pediatric patient with suspected epiglottitis is found sitting upright, leaning forward, drooling, and refusing to lie down. What is the most appropriate EMT action regarding positioning?
options: Immediately attempt to visualize the airway with a tongue depressor
Allow the child to remain in the position of comfort and avoid agitating them
Have the child lie on their back with legs elevated to treat for shock
Force the child to lie flat on the stretcher for a more thorough exam

q: Which finding is most concerning for a developing tension pneumothorax in a trauma patient?
options: Mild shortness of breath with equal breath sounds and stable vital signs
A respiratory rate of 16 with normal, unlabored breathing
A small, superficial laceration to the chest wall with no bruising
Worsening respiratory distress, absent breath sounds on one side, and tracheal deviation

q: Which presentation is most consistent with hypoglycemia in a known diabetic patient?
options: Kussmaul respirations with severe dehydration and gradual symptom onset
Rapid onset, cool/clammy skin, altered mental status, possible combativeness
A slow heart rate with high blood pressure and warm, flushed skin
Slow onset over hours to days, with warm, dry skin and a fruity breath odor

q: What is the primary mechanism causing altered mental status in a patient with diabetic ketoacidosis (severe hyperglycemia)?
options: Brain cells are starved of glucose because insulin isn't available to let it in
Elevated potassium directly impairing neuron function
Osmotic water shifts, dehydration, and acidosis disrupting brain function
Excess insulin causing brain cells to swell

q: Before assisting a patient with their own prescribed nitroglycerin, which of the following must be checked?
options: That the patient hasn't eaten any solid food within the last several hours
That the patient's systolic blood pressure is at or above about 100 mmHg
The patient's blood glucose level, to rule out hypoglycemia as the cause
That the patient's respiratory rate falls within a normal adult range

q: Which three findings make up the Cincinnati Prehospital Stroke Scale?
options: Pupil response, grip strength, gait
Headache, nausea, vomiting
Facial droop, arm drift, speech abnormality
Blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate

q: Which presentation in a patient with a known allergic exposure most strongly indicates anaphylaxis requiring epinephrine?
options: Mild itching at the exposure site only, with no rash or swelling
A single episode of sneezing with no skin or breathing changes
Widespread hives with respiratory distress and/or hypotension
Localized hives confined to the exposure site with no systemic symptoms

q: For adult CPR, the current recommended chest compression rate and depth are:
options: 140–160 per minute, at least 3 inches deep
Rate doesn't matter as long as depth is adequate
100–120 per minute, at least 2 inches deep
60–80 per minute, at least 1 inch deep

q: For a single rescuer performing adult CPR (no advanced airway in place), the compression-to-ventilation ratio is:
options: Continuous compressions with no ventilations ever

q: When using an AED, what should all rescuers do immediately before the device analyzes the rhythm?
options: Check a pulse manually before the AED does
Begin rescue breathing
Stop touching the patient ("clear" the patient)
Continue chest compressions during analysis

q: Which feature would most suggest a patient's chest pain is a myocardial infarction rather than stable angina?
options: Pain that has occurred identically many times before with the same resolution
Pain that persists despite rest and/or the patient's prescribed nitroglycerin
Pain that only occurs during physical exertion and never at rest
Pain that resolves completely with rest within a few minutes

q: Why is establishing the patient's "last known well" time critical in a suspected stroke?
options: It's mainly used to complete documentation and satisfy hospital paperwork requirements
It's only used for completing paperwork after the call is finished
Certain time-sensitive treatments depend heavily on how long the stroke has been occurring
It only determines which hospital's visiting hours apply to the family

q: After a generalized seizure ends, a patient is found confused, drowsy, and slow to respond. This is best described as:
options: The postictal state, a normal recovery period following a seizure
Definitive proof of a fever-related seizure
A sign the seizure is still ongoing and requires immediate intervention
A stroke that occurred during the seizure

q: The primary EMT priorities during an active generalized seizure are:
options: Physically restraining the patient's limbs to try to stop the convulsive movements
Protecting the patient from injury and protecting/maintaining the airway once the seizure stops
Inserting an oral airway between the teeth during the active convulsions
Giving the patient food or water immediately to prevent low blood sugar

q: Activated charcoal is generally most effective when given:
options: For ingested corrosive substances like bleach or acids
Relatively soon after ingestion of certain oral poisons, and per medical direction/protocol
Several hours after ingestion, once the substance has already been absorbed
For any type of poisoning as long as it's given before the patient reaches the hospital

q: Which combination of findings should raise the EMT's suspicion for sepsis in a patient with a known infection?
options: Fever or hypothermia, altered mental status, and signs of poor perfusion
Normal vital signs and full alertness with no change from baseline
A well-healed surgical scar with no redness or drainage
A single episode of sneezing with an otherwise normal exam

q: What is the EMT's role regarding a patient's abdominal pain in the field?
options: Determine the exact underlying diagnosis and its cause before initiating any transport
Delay transport in the field until a definitive diagnosis has been confirmed by exam
Recognize signs of a serious problem and transport promptly, not diagnose the exact cause
Give the patient food or water to see whether the abdominal symptoms improve

q: When approaching a patient experiencing a behavioral/psychiatric emergency who is agitated but not immediately violent, the EMT should generally:
options: Use a loud, commanding tone of voice to quickly assert control of the scene
Quickly reassure the patient that their concerns aren't serious, to keep things moving
Speak calmly, maintain a safe distance, and avoid sudden movements
Physically restrain the patient immediately as a precaution before assessment

q: An epinephrine auto-injector is typically administered:
options: Under the tongue, allowing it to dissolve
Into the forearm, over the muscle belly
Into the lateral thigh, mid-way between the hip and knee
Into the abdomen, just below and to the side of the navel

q: When assessing a dialysis patient, why is it important to avoid taking a blood pressure on the arm with the dialysis fistula/graft?
options: It's mainly a comfort measure since the cuff can feel uncomfortable over the fistula site
It can damage the fistula or occlude blood flow needed for dialysis
It usually causes a falsely elevated blood pressure reading
It's only a comfort preference for the patient, not a true medical concern

q: A patient with known sickle cell disease presenting with severe pain, particularly in the joints/long bones, is most likely experiencing:
options: An allergic reaction
A normal, expected daily symptom requiring no evaluation
A vaso-occlusive (sickle cell) pain crisis
A simple muscle strain

q: A young, anxious patient presents with rapid breathing, tingling in the fingers, and dizziness, with no other findings. What must the EMT do before assuming this is simple hyperventilation syndrome?
options: Immediately have the patient breathe into a paper bag with no further assessment
Ignore the symptoms since anxiety isn't a real medical concern
Rule out other serious causes of rapid breathing through thorough assessment first
Withhold oxygen since it isn't needed for anxiety-related symptoms

q: What is the current recommended first-line approach for severe, life-threatening external hemorrhage from an extremity?
options: Pressure points proximal to the wound only, avoiding any direct contact
A loosely wrapped bandage applied to avoid restricting distal circulation
Elevation of the limb above the level of the heart, without direct pressure
Direct pressure, with early tourniquet application for severe bleeding

q: A patient fell from a height of 15 feet and has an altered mental status. What secondary assessment approach is indicated?
options: No assessment needed until transport begins
A detailed exam limited to the head only
Rapid, full-body trauma assessment
Focused assessment of only the obviously injured area

q: For a trauma patient with a suspected spinal injury who is not breathing adequately, what airway maneuver should be used to open the airway?
options: Head-tilt, chin-lift
Sellick's maneuver (cricoid pressure)
No airway maneuver should be attempted
Jaw-thrust maneuver

q: What is the hallmark sign of a flail chest?
options: Paradoxical movement of a segment of the chest wall during breathing
Bruising isolated to the sternum with no palpable instability
Crepitus felt in the neck with no chest wall involvement
Absent breath sounds on one side only, with a normal respiratory rate

q: Which of the following is typically an EARLY sign of shock (compensated stage), rather than a late sign?
options: Absent radial pulses with a weak, thready carotid pulse
Hypotension with a systolic pressure well below normal
Tachycardia with a normal or only slightly low blood pressure
Unresponsiveness with agonal, gasping respirations

q: How should a completely amputated body part generally be managed and transported?
options: Packed directly in ice with no protective wrapping, risking frostbite to the tissue
Left at the scene, since reattachment is rarely successful and rarely attempted
Submerged directly in cold saline without any protective wrapping
Wrapped in a sterile dressing, placed in a plastic bag, and kept cool (not frozen) on ice

q: The general EMT approach to an impaled object (e.g., a knife left in a wound) is to:
options: Stabilize it in place with bulky dressings and leave removal to the hospital, with limited exceptions
Push it further into the wound in an attempt to tamponade and seal off the bleeding from within
Twist and manipulate it gently side to side to test and estimate how deep the object actually penetrates
Remove it immediately in the field to gain better direct control of the underlying source of bleeding

q: The initial management of an open (sucking) chest wound involves:
options: Packing the wound tightly with gauze and no dressing
Applying an occlusive or vented chest seal dressing
Applying a tourniquet around the chest
Leaving the wound completely uncovered

q: For an abdominal evisceration (organs protruding through a wound), the EMT should:
options: Cover the exposed organs with a moist, sterile dressing and not attempt to replace them
Apply a tourniquet above the wound to control bleeding from the organs
Leave the wound completely uncovered so the organs can "air out" and dry
Push the organs back into the abdominal cavity to reduce contamination risk

q: Using the adult "rule of nines," approximately what percentage of total body surface area does one entire arm represent?
When providing initial care for a thermal burn, cooling the burn with water is appropriate primarily to:
options: Stop the burning process and help relieve pain
Increase blood flow to the burned area to help flush out damaged tissue and speed healing
Submerge the entire body in ice water for at least 20 minutes to maximize the cooling effect
Wait until arrival at the emergency department, since field cooling can be handled more effectively there

q: Rising blood pressure, decreasing heart rate, and irregular respirations in a head-injured patient (Cushing's triad) suggest:
options: Findings consistent with a simple scalp laceration and no deeper intracranial injury
A normal compensatory response to hypovolemic shock, requiring no special concern
Increasing intracranial pressure — a serious, late, and worsening neurological sign
The patient is clinically stable and their neurological status is improving over time

q: Current EMS guidance on spinal motion restriction for trauma patients emphasizes:
options: Selective spinal motion restriction based on assessment criteria, rather than backboarding every trauma patient
Full spinal immobilization with a backboard for essentially every trauma patient, as a precaution
Restricting spinal motion only for patients who report neck or back pain
Restricting spinal motion based mainly on the mechanism of injury alone

q: Applying a pelvic binder to a patient with a suspected unstable pelvic fracture is done primarily to:
options: Make IV fluid resuscitation unnecessary for the rest of the call
Stabilize the pelvis and reduce internal hemorrhage by limiting further movement of fractured bone
Allow easier transport positioning by rigidly fixing the patient's legs together
Improve patient comfort during transport only, with no meaningful effect on internal bleeding

q: In a traumatic cardiac arrest, in addition to CPR, which intervention is a critical early priority if indicated?
options: Performing a detailed head-to-toe exam before any other assessment or intervention is even attempted
Delaying all interventions and withholding CPR until arrival at the hospital
Obtaining a full SAMPLE history from bystanders before beginning any hands-on care
Controlling severe external hemorrhage and addressing a suspected tension pneumothorax without delay

q: Which finding in a burn patient should raise the highest concern for airway involvement/inhalation injury?
options: Singed nasal hair, soot around the mouth/nose, or a hoarse voice
A superficial burn isolated to one hand with no other body areas involved
A patient who appears calm, asymptomatic, and is speaking in a normal voice
A burn that occurred outdoors in an open, well-ventilated area

q: Crush syndrome is a concern after prolonged entrapment/crush injury because:
options: It results from prolonged nerve compression causing lasting numbness in the limb
It has no systemic effects beyond the injured limb itself, so only local swelling should be expected
It mainly causes long-term bone healing problems in the injured limb
Toxins and potassium released from damaged muscle tissue can trigger dangerous heart rhythms and kidney damage once the limb is freed

q: An avulsed (knocked-out) permanent tooth should ideally be:
options: Discarded if it's been out of the mouth for more than a few minutes
Left dry and exposed to open air, which best preserves the root surface for reimplantation
Handled by the crown (not the root) and placed in an appropriate storage medium such as milk or saline
Scrubbed clean with soap and water before being wrapped and stored for transport

q: Why should EMTs generally avoid hyperventilating (over-ventilating) a patient with a traumatic brain injury?
options: It is generally recommended for any patient with a suspected brain injury
Excessive ventilation lowers CO2 and causes cerebral vasoconstriction, potentially worsening brain injury outcomes
It only affects oxygenation levels, not intracranial pressure or blood flow
It improves oxygenation enough to outweigh any effect on intracranial pressure

q: Which sign is considered an early, key warning sign of developing compartment syndrome in an injured limb?
options: A normal, mild ache that resolves completely with rest and elevation of the limb
Slight bruising with no pain, tenderness, or swelling of the affected limb
Pain out of proportion to the apparent injury, especially with passive stretching
Warm, well-perfused skin with strong distal pulses and no patient complaints at all

q: What is considered a normal heart rate for a healthy newborn immediately after birth?
options: 200–220 bpm, similar to a rapid supraventricular tachycardia
100–180 bpm, generally in the range of about 120–160
40–60 bpm, similar to a resting healthy adult
Less than 40 bpm, a rate seen only in profound bradycardia

q: The APGAR score evaluates a newborn's condition based on which five components?
options: Appearance, Pain response, Gestational age, Activity, Respirations
Apnea, Pulse, Gag reflex, Alertness, Reflexes
Appearance, Pulse, Grimace, Activity, Respirations
Airway, Pulse, Glucose, Alertness, Reflexes

q: For a newly born infant who is not breathing adequately, the first steps in resuscitation generally are:
options: Immediate intubation for any newborn who doesn't cry right after delivery
Dry, warm, stimulate, and position/clear the airway, then reassess breathing
Immediate chest compressions before any other assessment or intervention is attempted
Begin rescue breathing on all newborns as a precaution before assessing them

q: The Pediatric Assessment Triangle (PAT) evaluates which three components from across the room, before hands-on contact?
options: Appearance, work of breathing, circulation to skin
SAMPLE history, OPQRST, and a full set of baseline vital signs
Weight, age, immunization status
Blood pressure, pulse, respirations

q: Compared to adults, healthy children generally have:
options: Slower heart rates and slower respiratory rates
Lower blood pressure with a faster heart rate only after age 12
Vital signs similar to adults once they reach school age
Faster heart rates and faster respiratory rates than adults

q: Compared to adults, a child's airway is:
options: Proportionally smaller, with a larger tongue and a higher, more anterior larynx, making obstruction more likely
Proportionally larger than an adult's, making it significantly less prone to obstruction or swelling
Similar in shape to an adult's, just smaller in overall size
Less flexible cartilage that is more prone to fracture than an adult's airway structures

q: A febrile seizure in a young child is generally defined as:
options: A seizure that only occurs in adults who have a long history of chronic, untreated fevers
A permanent neurological condition that persists and requires lifelong anticonvulsant therapy
A seizure that is completely unrelated to body temperature or any recent illness
A seizure from a rapid rise in body temperature, most common around 6 months to 5 years old

q: Which finding in an infant should raise concern for possible abusive head trauma?
options: A clear, consistent history from the caregiver that matches the type and severity of the injury seen
A minor bruise on the shin of a toddler who is actively learning to walk and frequently falls
A vague, inconsistent history that doesn't match the injury, or injuries beyond the child's developmental stage
Normal, age-appropriate behavior and development with no visible injury of any kind

q: Why should a pregnant patient in the third trimester generally avoid lying flat on her back for extended periods?
options: It's mainly recommended to reduce lower back strain during transport
It only affects fetal movement and positioning, with absolutely no impact on maternal circulation or blood pressure
It has no physiological effect on a pregnant patient's circulation or blood pressure at all
The uterus can compress the inferior vena cava, reducing blood return to the heart and causing hypotension

q: If the umbilical cord is visibly protruding from the vagina before delivery of the baby (prolapsed cord), the EMT should:
options: Attempt to push the cord back inside the vagina to reduce the prolapse before transport
Pull firmly and steadily on the visible cord to help assist and considerably speed up the overall delivery process
Continue with a normal delivery timeline, since the cord will usually reposition on its own
Position the mother to relieve pressure on the cord, keep it moist, and transport immediately as an emergency

q: Elderly patients experiencing a myocardial infarction are more likely than younger patients to present with:
options: Atypical symptoms such as shortness of breath, fatigue, or confusion, with little or no chest pain
Classic, severe crushing chest pain radiating to the arm in essentially every case
Symptoms that closely mirror the classic crushing chest pain seen in younger patients
Very mild, brief chest discomfort that resolves on its own within seconds

q: Which finding should raise an EMT's suspicion for possible elder abuse or neglect?
options: A single, explained bruise consistent with a witnessed fall
A clean, well-cared-for living environment with fresh food and properly stored medications
A patient who is fully alert, cooperative, and reports no concerns during private conversation
Multiple injuries in different healing stages, poor hygiene, or a caregiver blocking private conversation

q: When caring for a patient with autism spectrum disorder, an EMT should generally:
options: Minimize sensory stimulation, use clear and simple language, and allow extra time and patience
Physically restrain the patient immediately upon contact to prevent unpredictable movement
Assume the patient cannot understand anything being said and speak only to caregivers
Use a loud, firm voice with rapid, complex sentences to establish authority quickly

q: When planning to move and transport a bariatric (severely obese) patient, an important early EMT consideration is:
options: It requires no different planning, equipment, or staffing than any other routine patient
Requesting additional resources such as a bariatric stretcher and extra personnel proactively before the move
Assuming that standard equipment and normal crew staffing will always be sufficient
Delaying any assessment or intervention until extra staff arrive, even if the patient is critically unstable

q: Which finding would be a concerning sign of significant dehydration in an infant?
options: A bulging, tense fontanelle along with excessive tearing and increased urine output
Frequent wet diapers with clear, pale urine throughout the day
Normal, moist mucous membranes with good skin turgor and no change in behavior
A sunken fontanelle, dry mucous membranes, and decreased urine output

q: When positioning an ambulance at a motor vehicle collision on a roadway, a key safety principle is to:
options: Rely on hazard lights alone without positioning the ambulance defensively
Park as close to the wreckage as possible to minimize the distance to carry equipment
Position the ambulance to protect the scene from oncoming traffic, using appropriate warning devices
Block all lanes of traffic as a standard practice at every collision scene

q: In a multiple-casualty incident, the first-arriving EMS unit's initial priority is generally to:
options: Perform a scene size-up, establish command, and request additional resources before treating a single patient
Wait for all other responding units to arrive before taking any action at all
Begin immediate, detailed treatment of the first patient encountered, ignoring the rest of the scene
Transport the single most severely injured patient immediately, without waiting for backup

q: Basic START triage categorizes patients using which general framework?
options: Only two categories are used in the field: patients who are alive and patients who are deceased
Based mainly on the patient's age, treating children and elderly patients as higher priority by default
Based on treating whichever patients are found first during the initial walk-through
Immediate, Delayed, Minor, Deceased/Expectant, based on walking ability, breathing, perfusion, and mental status

q: During vehicle extrication, the EMT's general priority regarding patient care is to:
options: Encourage the patient to self-extricate whenever they are able, before any assessment
Gain access and begin critical assessment and interventions as soon as safely possible, before full extrication
Wait until the vehicle doors can be fully opened before beginning any care
Wait until the patient is completely removed from the vehicle before any assessment or care begins

q: When arriving at a scene with a suspected hazardous materials release, the EMT's first priority is to:
options: Stage at a safe distance, avoid the hazard zone without proper training/equipment, and request specialized resources
Approach directly and immediately to assess for patients without confirming the hazard first
Use smell and visual clues to identify the substance before deciding whether to approach
Enter quickly to begin patient care, since delays could worsen outcomes

q: Which of the following is a recognized, normal acute stress reaction an EMT might experience after a difficult call?
options: Symptoms like difficulty sleeping, irritability, or intrusive thoughts
Staying completely calm and unaffected afterward is the healthiest way to handle a difficult call
These reactions are best kept private and worked through on your own
These reactions mean the EMT is unfit for the job and should consider resigning

q: A primary purpose of the prehospital care report (PCR) is to:
options: Provide an accurate legal and medical record of the call, supporting continuity of care and QA review
Replace the need for a verbal handoff report to hospital staff at the bedside
Only need to be completed if the patient is actually transported to the hospital
Serve mainly as a billing document required by the receiving facility

q: For a competent adult patient to legally refuse care/transport, they generally must:
options: State their refusal verbally, without needing to sign any paperwork
Have a family member co-sign the refusal form in addition to the patient
Refusal of care is only valid if witnessed and signed by a law enforcement officer
Be of legal age (or emancipated), mentally competent, and informed of the risks of refusing care

q: "Implied consent" in EMS generally applies to:
options: Every patient contact regardless of their condition, competence, or ability to communicate
An unresponsive or incapacitated patient who cannot give informed consent, assumed to want life-saving treatment
Only patients who have signed a specific written consent form well in advance, notarized by a witness
Only pediatric patients, since minors cannot legally provide informed consent themselves

q: In EMS, "abandonment" refers to:
options: Refusing to accept a new call while already treating another patient
Any time a patient is transferred to a hospital and handed off to emergency department staff
Following a patient's valid, informed refusal of care after proper risk disclosure and documentation were completed
Terminating care without ensuring an equal or higher level of care continues, and without the patient's consent

q: For an EMT to be found legally negligent, which of the following must generally be demonstrated?
options: EMS providers are legally immune from negligence claims while on duty
Only that the patient was unhappy with the care they received during transport
Only that the provider deviated from protocol, even if the patient wasn't harmed
Duty to act, breach of that duty, damages, and causation connecting the breach to the damages

q: Why is using clear, plain-language communication (rather than agency-specific codes) especially important during a multi-agency response?
options: Plain language is mainly reserved for public-facing announcements, not tactical radio traffic
It mainly matters for documentation purposes, not real-time communication
Codes are generally quicker and used consistently across most agencies
It reduces confusion between agencies/departments that may use different code systems

q: When establishing a landing zone for a medical helicopter, a key safety consideration is:
options: Any size or surface, flat or not, is acceptable as long as it's near the scene
Landing zones should be as close to the patient as possible, even if the surface isn't ideal
Selecting an adequately sized, relatively flat, obstruction-free area, and keeping bystanders and loose objects clear
Helicopters can land safely anywhere at all without any ground crew coordination, communication, or hazard assessment

q: When responding to a call involving suspected domestic violence, an important EMT safety consideration is:
options: Assuming the scene stays safe for the rest of the call once law enforcement has cleared it
Interviewing the patient in front of the suspected abuser to save time
Remaining alert that the situation could become volatile again, and following scene safety protocols throughout contact
Only involving law enforcement if the patient specifically requests it

q: A patient's medical information gathered during an EMS call should generally be shared:
options: With immediate family members by default, since they're usually considered part of the care team
Only with those directly involved in the patient's care, or as otherwise legally required/authorized
Publicly, whenever the call was interesting or noteworthy enough to share
Freely with anyone who asks, including friends, family, or on social media platforms

q: The Glasgow Coma Scale evaluates which three components?
options: Eye opening, verbal response, motor response
Pupil size, pupil reactivity, and conjugate gaze position
Pulse, respirations, blood pressure
Skin color, temperature, moisture

q: A Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15 indicates:
options: The patient is fully alert and oriented, with no deficits in the components measured
The score is invalid and the assessment must be immediately re-checked
The patient is in a deep, unresponsive coma with no purposeful movement or reflexes present
The patient is completely unresponsive to any verbal or painful stimulus

q: Assessing distal pulses, motor function, and sensation (PMS) in an injured limb is done primarily to:
options: Determine the patient's overall pain tolerance and threshold for treatment
Evaluate for possible nerve or vascular compromise from the injury
Determine whether a splint is needed at all before any further exam
Decide which specific hospital the patient should be transported to

q: Asking a patient their name, where they are, the approximate date, and what happened to them assesses:
options: Their respiratory effort, rate, and depth of breathing
Their capillary refill time at the nail beds
Their subjective pain scale rating on a scale of zero to ten
Their level of orientation (person, place, time, event)

q: On approaching a motor vehicle collision with a downed power line across the vehicle, the EMT should:
options: Approach immediately to assess and begin treating the patient inside the vehicle without delay
Move the downed line out of the way yourself using a nearby wooden pole
Stage at a safe distance and wait for confirmation the line is de-energized before approaching
Instruct the patient to exit the vehicle immediately and walk to safety

q: Which of the following would generally be considered a significant mechanism of injury warranting a rapid trauma assessment?
options: A stubbed toe
Ejection from a vehicle
A minor fall from standing height with no injury complaints
A low-speed fender bender with no complaints

q: The concept sometimes called the "golden period" in trauma care refers to:
options: A specific billing time frame used only for insurance reimbursement purposes
The time it takes for a crew to complete all required paperwork after finishing a call
A specific one-hour time limit required by protocol for reaching a trauma center
The general principle that minimizing time to definitive care improves outcomes for seriously injured patients

q: A key EMT principle is to treat based on assessment findings rather than a specific diagnosis. This means:
options: Objective exam findings should be ignored in favor of the patient's own self-diagnosis
Diagnosis and treatment are considered the exact same thing in prehospital EMS care
EMTs should identify the specific disease process before beginning treatment
EMTs manage what they find, like poor perfusion or inadequate breathing, without needing a diagnosis

q: In a patient with chest pain, documenting that the patient denies shortness of breath, nausea, or radiation of pain is an example of:
options: An irrelevant detail that shouldn't ever be documented in the patient care report
A vital sign measurement taken during the initial assessment
A mechanism of injury noted from the scene size-up
A pertinent negative, which is a relevant part of the patient's history

q: Why is it important to trend vital signs (compare them over time) rather than relying on a single set?
options: A changing trend can reveal a deteriorating patient even if any one reading looks acceptable
Vital signs typically stay stable enough during a single call that repeat checks rarely add value
Trending vital signs is only useful for healthy patients
A single set of vital signs is usually enough to understand a patient's status

q: In a trauma patient where you cannot immediately get a blood pressure reading, the presence of a palpable radial pulse suggests:
options: The heart rate must be below 60 beats per minute at that moment
A rough estimate that systolic blood pressure is at least approximately 80-90 mmHg or higher
The systolic blood pressure is critically low, almost certainly below 60 mmHg at this point
The patient has no perfusion at all and is in profound decompensated shock

q: When a patient's history is unreliable or unavailable (e.g., due to altered mental status with no bystanders), the EMT should:
options: Delay treatment until family or bystanders can be located to provide a history
Rely on physical exam findings, scene clues, and any available secondary sources to guide care
Assume the patient is faking their symptoms and requires no further assessment
Delay all treatment indefinitely until a reliable historian can be located

q: For a responsive medical patient (as opposed to trauma), the assessment generally emphasizes:
options: A history of the present illness and focused physical exam directed at the chief complaint
A rapid head-to-toe exam like the one used for trauma patients
Obtaining vital signs first, before asking about the chief complaint
Only assessing the specific areas the patient physically points to and nothing else

q: For an unresponsive medical patient with an unknown cause, which assessment approach is generally indicated?
options: Only a discussion with family members, without ever touching or examining the patient
A physical exam is optional for medical patients as long as bystanders provide a history
A rapid full-body physical exam, similar in scope to a trauma patient, since the cause is unknown
A focused exam limited to a single body system related to the chief complaint

q: Arriving at a residence following a report of a structural collapse, the EMT's first priority before entering is to:
options: Ensure the structure has been assessed as safe to enter by trained personnel before entry
Wait indefinitely at the perimeter with no assessment or communication at all
Rush in immediately to begin treating any visible or audible patients inside the structure
Enter the structure only if patients inside are audibly screaming for help

q: Which of the following best describes adequate breathing in an adult?
options: Any respiratory rate above 40 breaths per minute, since faster breathing means more oxygen intake
Shallow, rapid breaths accompanied by visible retractions at the neck and ribs
A rate and depth sufficient for normal oxygenation, with regular rhythm and equal chest rise
Slow, gasping, irregular breaths with long pauses between each breath

q: Visible retractions (skin pulling in around the ribs/neck with each breath) in a child are a sign of:
options: Adequate oxygenation and ventilation with no clinical concern at all
A full stomach from swallowing air during crying
Normal, effortless breathing effort with no accessory muscle use
Increased work of breathing, indicating significant respiratory distress

q: A high-pitched sound heard during inspiration, known as stridor, is most concerning for:
options: Upper airway obstruction/narrowing
Fluid in the lower lungs only
A completely normal breath sound
Lower airway constriction, like asthma

q: Rales (crackles) heard on lung auscultation are often associated with:
options: Fluid in the alveoli, such as in pulmonary edema or pneumonia
A pneumothorax exclusively, with absent breath sounds on one side
Upper airway obstruction only, with no involvement of the lower airways
A completely clear, healthy lung with no adventitious sounds present

q: Wheezing is most commonly associated with:
options: A sign of cardiac arrest and absent circulation
A normal, expected finding in every healthy patient at rest
A foreign body lodged in the upper airway, causing partial obstruction
Narrowing of the lower airways, such as in asthma or COPD

q: A non-rebreather mask should generally be run at a flow rate of approximately:
options: As low a flow as possible to conserve the oxygen tank's supply
At least 10-15 LPM, enough to keep the reservoir bag inflated
A low flow of only 1-2 LPM, similar to what's used with a nasal cannula
A fixed 6 LPM, the same starting rate used for a nasal cannula

q: A nasal cannula is generally used at flow rates of approximately:
options: 1-6 LPM
Up to 15 LPM, similar to a non-rebreather mask
25 LPM
15 LPM only

q: Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP) is most commonly used for patients with:
options: A patient in cardiac arrest with no pulse and no spontaneous respiratory effort at all
A patient with a complete airway obstruction who needs immediate manual clearing of the airway
A patient with mild shortness of breath but normal oxygen saturation and no distress
Moderate to severe respiratory distress with adequate mental status and effort, often from pulmonary edema or COPD

q: CPAP is generally contraindicated or used with caution in which situation?
options: A patient in respiratory distress who is alert and can protect their airway
A patient who simply requests the CPAP mask without any respiratory distress present
A patient with only mild shortness of breath, a normal mental status, and no signs of distress
A patient with a decreased level of consciousness who cannot protect their own airway, or who has a suspected pneumothorax

q: Why is two-rescuer BVM ventilation generally considered more effective than one-rescuer technique?
options: It allows one rescuer to maintain a proper mask seal while the other squeezes the bag, improving tidal volume delivery
It uses noticeably less oxygen from the tank per breath, meaningfully extending how long a full cylinder will last
It means only one rescuer needs to worry about head tilt and jaw thrust, since bagging alone keeps the airway open
It is mandated by law as a legal requirement in every state for any positive-pressure ventilation performed on a patient

q: After beginning BVM ventilations, which finding would suggest the ventilations are NOT adequate?
options: Improving skin color and rising oxygen saturation
A steady, appropriate ventilation rate with a good mask seal
No visible chest rise and no improvement in oxygen saturation
Equal, visible chest rise with each squeeze at an appropriate rate

q: Excessive ventilation volume or rate with a BVM can lead to:
options: A guaranteed improvement in oxygenation with no downsides
Gastric distention, increasing the risk of vomiting and aspiration
Immediate cure of the underlying respiratory problem
No physiological effect at all on the patient's stomach or lungs

q: The recovery position (lateral recumbent) is used for a breathing, unresponsive patient primarily to:
options: Increase the patient's blood pressure back toward a normal range through improved venous return
Improve the effectiveness of chest compressions being performed on a patient lying supine on a firm surface
Prepare the patient for full spinal immobilization on a backboard prior to transport to the hospital
Help protect the airway from aspiration if the patient vomits, while still allowing adequate breathing

q: In a patient with severe COPD, oxygen administration should generally be:
options: Given at the highest flow rate available, since more oxygen is generally considered better for a patient in respiratory distress
Titrated to relieve hypoxia while still being attentive to the patient's respiratory drive and response, per protocol
Withheld unless the patient is in obvious severe distress, since supplemental oxygen can suppress a COPD patient's drive to breathe
Only given once the patient reports feeling short of breath, rather than based on oxygen saturation readings

q: For a conscious infant with a complete airway obstruction, the recommended technique is:
options: Sweeping the mouth blindly with a finger
Abdominal thrusts, the same as an adult
No intervention until the infant becomes unresponsive
A combination of back blows and chest thrusts

q: The "Chain of Survival" for cardiac arrest generally includes which sequence of concepts?
options: Early recognition/activation of EMS, early CPR, early defibrillation, early advanced care, and post-arrest care
Focusing only on 2-minute cycles of compressions between rhythm checks, without addressing early defibrillation or advanced care
Calling for help only after starting CPR, once the first few cycles of compressions are done
Only early defibrillation matters; recognition and CPR are not important steps

q: "Return of spontaneous circulation" (ROSC) refers to:
options: The moment an AED is applied to the patient's chest, before any shock is delivered
The patient regaining a palpable pulse and organized cardiac activity after cardiac arrest
The exact moment chest compressions and CPR are first begun on the patient
A permanently fixed neurological outcome determined at the scene of the arrest

q: Standard AED pad placement for an adult is generally:
options: Pad placement does not matter at all, as long as they touch the skin somewhere
Both pads placed directly over the sternum, stacked one above the other
One pad on the upper right chest, one pad on the lower left side/ribcage (or per pad diagram)
Both pads placed on the same side of the chest, several inches apart

q: Which of the following is a generally recognized reason to stop CPR in the field?
options: The rescuer feels momentarily tired but is still physically able to continue compressions
CPR should be continued until the patient reaches the hospital, even if a valid DNR is discovered mid-call
After a fixed 20-minute period of CPR with no return of pulse, regardless of other factors
Return of spontaneous circulation, arrival of higher-level care who assumes responsibility, or valid orders to stop

q: Why is allowing full chest recoil between compressions important during CPR?
options: It slows the overall compression rate down well below the currently recommended target range
It is only relevant for pediatric patients and does not meaningfully apply to adult CPR at all
It allows the heart to refill with blood between compressions, improving subsequent compression effectiveness
It mainly gives the rescuer a brief moment to rest between compressions

q: Why does current guidance emphasize minimizing interruptions in chest compressions?
options: Interruptions are required every 30 seconds by protocol to reassess the airway
Interruptions improve oxygenation by giving the lungs a brief rest period
Even brief pauses reduce blood flow and coronary perfusion pressure, which take time to rebuild
Interruptions have no measurable effect on outcomes as long as they're brief

q: When assessing a patient with chest pain using OPQRST, asking "does the pain radiate anywhere, like to your arm or jaw?" corresponds to which component?
options: Time
Onset
Radiation
Severity

q: Diabetic patients are more likely than the general population to experience myocardial infarction with:
options: No cardiac risk at all, since diabetes doesn't affect the heart
Classic, severe crushing chest pain that is present in nearly all cases
Symptoms that closely mirror those of a diabetic emergency like hypoglycemia, rather than a typical cardiac presentation
Little or no chest pain (a "silent" MI), due to diabetes-related nerve changes

q: Aspirin is often given (per protocol) to patients with suspected acute coronary syndrome primarily because it:
options: Works quickly to relieve the chest pain itself, similar to how nitroglycerin acts
Has no relevant pharmacological effect on the patient in this situation
Lowers the patient's blood pressure significantly within a few minutes
Has an antiplatelet effect that may help limit clot formation contributing to the blockage

q: For a conscious, alert diabetic patient with confirmed hypoglycemia who can safely swallow, appropriate initial management often includes:
options: Withholding all treatment until ALS arrives
Aggressive hyperventilation
Immediate IV insulin
Oral glucose or a sugar source, per protocol

q: For a hypoglycemic patient who is unresponsive and unable to protect their airway, the EMT should NOT:
options: Place oral glucose or any substance directly into the mouth of an unresponsive patient, due to aspiration risk
Position the patient to protect the airway, such as placing them in a lateral recovery position
Monitor the airway closely and continuously for any early signs of vomiting or developing obstruction
Request ALS/advanced care as appropriate so glucose can be given by an alternate route such as IV or IM

q: In general terms, the two broad categories of stroke are:
options: Ischemic (blocked blood flow) and hemorrhagic (bleeding into the brain)
Only hemorrhagic strokes exist; ischemic stroke is not a real category
Viral and bacterial strokes, caused by infectious organisms
Only ischemic strokes exist; hemorrhagic stroke is not a real category

q: Why is aspirin generally NOT given by EMTs for suspected stroke symptoms (unlike suspected cardiac chest pain)?
options: Aspirin is generally more effective at treating stroke symptoms than it is for cardiac chest pain
A stroke could be hemorrhagic, so aspirin's antiplatelet effect might worsen bleeding before the stroke type is confirmed
Aspirin has no relevant pharmacological properties that would meaningfully affect any stroke patient at all
Stroke protocols generally call for the same antiplatelet therapy as cardiac chest pain, just with closer monitoring

q: A brief seizure characterized by a blank stare and momentary loss of awareness, without dramatic convulsive movements, is most consistent with:
options: A febrile seizure exclusively
An absence seizure
Status epilepticus
A generalized tonic-clonic seizure

q: "Status epilepticus" generally refers to:
options: A single seizure that occurred years ago with no current activity or symptoms
A prolonged seizure or repeated seizures without full recovery in between, a serious emergency
A chronic seizure disorder diagnosis given after a patient has had several seizures over their lifetime
A single, brief seizure lasting only a few seconds, followed by full recovery

q: The classic presentation of an opioid/narcotic overdose includes:
options: Rapid, deep breathing along with an elevated heart rate
Pinpoint (constricted) pupils, slow/shallow breathing, decreased level of consciousness
A high fever combined with active seizures, and nothing else
Dilated pupils, rapid breathing, and significant agitation or combativeness

q: Naloxone works by:
options: Directly increasing the patient's blood sugar to correct hypoglycemia
Sedating an agitated patient to reduce combativeness during transport
Stopping all active bleeding anywhere in the patient's body
Reversing the effects of opioids by blocking/displacing them from their receptors

q: At the scene of a suspected overdose, it's valuable for EMS to look for:
options: Pill bottles or drug paraphernalia at the scene that could indicate the substance involved
Focusing scene time only on interviewing bystanders, since physical evidence rarely changes patient care
The patient's insurance card only, since that determines the hospital destination
Nothing beyond the patient's vital signs, since scene clues rarely change treatment

q: A key feature that helps distinguish heat stroke from heat exhaustion is:
options: Both conditions are managed with the same cooling steps, so distinguishing between them isn't clinically important
Heat exhaustion typically involves more severe alterations in mental status than heat stroke
Heat stroke typically involves altered mental status or significant neurological changes, unlike heat exhaustion
Heat stroke is diagnosed mainly by core body temperature alone, without needing to assess mental status

q: A patient with severe hypothermia should generally be handled:
options: Only while vigorously exercising the patient's arms and legs to generate body heat quickly
Gently, since rough handling can trigger a dangerous cardiac arrhythmia in a severely hypothermic heart
The same as any other alert, conscious patient, with no special precautions needed at all
Roughly, since careful or gentle handling doesn't matter once a patient is hypothermic

q: A "contrecoup" brain injury occurs when:
options: The brain is injured directly beneath the site of impact from the initial blow
The term applies specifically to penetrating injuries where the object passes through and exits the opposite side of the skull
The brain is injured on the side opposite the point of impact, as it moves and strikes the opposite skull
There is bruising to the scalp only, without deeper brain tissue involvement

q: Understanding the "kinematics of trauma" (how the injury likely occurred) helps the EMT primarily by:
options: Determining who is legally at fault for causing the incident on scene, for the report
Determining which specific transport billing codes apply to this particular call
Replacing the need for any hands-on physical assessment of the patient at all, ever
Predicting likely injury patterns from the mechanism, guiding assessment before all injuries are visible

q: The key distinction between blunt and penetrating trauma is:
options: There is no meaningful clinical difference at all between the two trauma mechanisms
Penetrating trauma means an object enters the body through broken skin; blunt trauma need not break the skin
Blunt trauma typically involves an object breaking the skin, similar to a penetrating injury
Penetrating trauma generally causes less internal injury than blunt trauma, since the force is concentrated at a single point

q: In a gunshot wound, which statement is generally most accurate?
options: EMTs should focus on determining exact wound trajectories rather than treating the patient
Exit wounds are generally smaller and more precise than entrance wounds, since exiting tissue offers less resistance
Gunshot wounds typically have only a single identifiable wound, since entrance and exit points usually overlap
Exit wounds, when present, are often larger and more irregular than entrance wounds

q: A basic principle of splinting a long bone fracture is to:
options: Apply the splint snugly enough to fully eliminate any movement at the fracture site, even if it feels tight
Immobilize the joint above and the joint below the injury site
Assess pulses, motor function, and sensation only after the splint has been fully applied
Immobilize only the exact point of the fracture

q: A traction splint is generally indicated for:
options: A suspected fracture of the forearm with significant deformity and swelling
An open fracture located near the knee joint itself, in most local EMS protocols
A suspected hip fracture with significant joint involvement and visible deformity present
A closed, isolated mid-shaft femur fracture with no joint or pelvic involvement, per local protocol

q: Distal pulse, motor function, and sensation (PMS) should be checked:
options: Both before and after splinting, to detect any change caused by the splinting process
Once before splinting and once more only if the patient reports new pain
Only after the patient reaches the hospital, not before or during transport
PMS checks are not relevant to splinting and can safely be skipped

q: Traumatic asphyxia, sometimes seen after severe crush injury to the chest, is characterized by:
options: A pattern of injury seen mainly in the abdomen following seatbelt-related compression
Severe bruising/discoloration and swelling of the head, neck, and upper chest from sudden chest compression
A finding typically associated with penetrating trauma to the chest rather than blunt compression
Localized bruising limited only to the direct point of chest impact, with no involvement above the collarbone

q: A patient with multiple rib fractures on one side is at risk for which associated complications?
options: Mainly localized pain at the fracture site, without significant risk to the lungs beneath
A near-certain risk of flail chest requiring immediate needle decompression before transport
Underlying lung injury such as pneumothorax or hemothorax, and pain limiting adequate breathing
Only minor skin bruising directly over the fracture site, with no deeper structures ever being involved

q: A hemothorax refers to:
options: Fluid buildup around the heart that restricts its ability to pump effectively
Air accumulating within the pleural space, which causes the lung on that side to collapse inward
Blood accumulating in the pleural space, which can compress the lung and affect breathing
A minor, self-resolving finding that typically doesn't require any additional monitoring

q: Which finding in a patient with blunt abdominal trauma would raise the highest concern for significant internal bleeding?
options: Mild surface bruising with no other findings
A rigid, distended, tender abdomen with signs of shock
A normal, soft, non-tender abdomen with normal vital signs
A patient who reports feeling fine and remains alert with stable initial vital signs

q: For trauma involving the external genitalia, the EMT's general approach includes:
options: Applying a tourniquet around the pelvis for any significant external bleeding in this region
Deferring any bleeding control there until after treating more visible injuries elsewhere on the body
Applying only a light dressing initially, and saving more thorough bleeding control for the hospital
Controlling bleeding with direct pressure/dressings as appropriate, maintaining patient dignity and privacy

q: The initial priority in managing a near-drowning patient is:
options: Withholding all rescue breathing in every drowning case until ALS arrives on scene
Immediate full spinal immobilization before any airway or breathing interventions, regardless of the diving history
Focusing first on removing wet clothing and warming the patient before addressing airway and breathing
Removing the patient from the water and addressing airway/breathing, with spinal precautions based on mechanism

q: For a traumatic eye injury with the eye partially avulsed from its socket, the EMT should generally:
options: Push the eye firmly back into its socket to reposition it before bandaging it securely in place
Irrigate the eye forcefully with a firehose-strength stream of water sustained for several minutes
Protect the eye in place with a moist dressing and rigid shield, without pressure, and transport promptly
Apply firm, direct manual pressure to the globe itself in an attempt to control any active bleeding

q: The initial management of a chemical burn to the skin generally involves:
options: Rubbing the burned area vigorously with a dry cloth to remove residue
Leaving the chemical in place and transporting immediately with no decontamination
Removing contaminated clothing and irrigating the area with large amounts of water, per protocol
Applying a neutralizing chemical agent directly onto the burned area

q: Electrical injuries are notable because:
options: Visible burns at entry/exit points may be small while significant internal damage can still be present
They are typically minor if there's no visible burn present, requiring only basic first aid
Electrical injuries mainly affect the skin and muscles, with cardiac involvement being extremely rare
The visible skin injury at the entry and exit points is generally the best indicator of how much internal damage occurred

q: When responding to a lightning strike incident, EMS providers should:
options: Remain aware the scene may be unsafe if the storm continues, and take shelter before extended care
Assume there is no ongoing risk to responders once one strike has already occurred
Focus first on patient care, since a single lightning strike makes a second strike in the same spot unlikely
Stand out in the open at the highest point of the area for a clearer better view

q: In a patient with multiple, significant injuries (multi-system trauma), the EMT's priority is generally to:
options: Prioritize identifying and managing immediate life threats (airway, breathing, bleeding) first
Only ever treat whichever single injury happens to look the most visually dramatic
Address each visible injury in the order it's found, working from head to toe
Complete a full detailed physical exam before beginning treatment of any identified injury

q: A general principle in suspected sports-related concussion is:
options: The athlete should be removed from play and evaluated
Concussions in youth sports usually resolve within a day or two without needing formal evaluation
The athlete should immediately return to play whenever they insist that they feel fine
No assessment is needed at all if the athlete is still able to walk unassisted

q: For most wounds with embedded surface debris (not a true impaled object), general initial EMS management involves:
options: Removing any visible debris from the wound bed before applying a dressing
Covering the wound loosely without applying direct pressure, since bleeding control isn't usually a concern with surface debris
Suturing the wound completely closed in the field before transport even begins
Controlling bleeding and covering the wound per protocol, without digging out deeply embedded material

q: The first stage of labor is generally defined as beginning with:
options: The cutting and clamping of the umbilical cord after delivery
The onset of regular contractions and cervical dilation, ending with full dilation
The delivery of the placenta, which follows the baby's birth
The moment of the baby's first audible cry immediately after birth

q: "Crowning" refers to:
options: The delivery of the placenta, which happens after the baby is fully born
The baby's head or presenting part becoming visible at the opening, indicating imminent delivery
The mother's contractions first beginning, very early in the labor process
A complication that requires immediate emergency surgery in all cases

q: Drying and stimulating a newborn immediately after birth serves to:
options: Primarily help clean the baby, since respiratory effort is expected to have already started by delivery
Mainly serve a comfort purpose, since a newborn's breathing typically starts on its own regardless of drying or stimulation
Replace the need for any further assessment of the newborn's condition
Help prevent heat loss and often stimulates the newborn to begin breathing effectively

q: A breech presentation refers to:
options: The baby's head presenting first at the vaginal opening, as is typical and expected
The umbilical cord presenting first, ahead of any part of the baby itself
A common variant of labor that generally doesn't increase risk to the baby during delivery
The baby's buttocks or feet presenting first instead of the head

q: Initial EMS management of significant postpartum (after-delivery) bleeding often includes:
options: Withholding all treatment and transport until arrival at the hospital's ED
Uterine massage (per protocol) and treating for shock as appropriate, along with prompt transport
Ignoring the bleeding since it's expected after delivery
Packing the vaginal opening with gauze dressings to help control the bleeding

q: Length-based resuscitation tapes (such as a Broselow tape) are used in pediatric emergencies primarily to:
options: Estimate a child's weight from their length/height, guiding equipment sizing and medication dosing
Replace the need for any hands-on physical assessment of the child at all
Measure the child's exact chronological age in years, months, and days
Determine which specific hospital the child should ultimately be transported to

q: In children, cardiac arrest is more often the end result of:
options: An event most often triggered by a primary cardiac arrhythmia, similar to what's typically seen in adults
A primary cardiac event, just as it is in adults, in the clear majority of cases
A condition usually caused by choking on a foreign object as the sole underlying mechanism
A respiratory problem that progresses to cardiac arrest if untreated, more often than cardiac causes

q: Croup in a young child classically presents with:
options: Severe abdominal pain
Chest pain radiating to the arm
A barking cough and stridor, often worse at night
A sudden high fever with drooling and an inability to swallow

q: For a child with a fever but no other concerning findings, the EMT's general approach includes:
options: A thorough assessment for any red-flag findings, supportive care, and transport per protocol/parental wishes
Immediate aggressive cooling with full ice water immersion applied in absolutely every febrile case seen
Focusing the assessment solely on measuring temperature, since the exact number best predicts how serious the illness is
Treating the fever with over-the-counter antipyretics on scene as the primary intervention, before transport

q: When caring for a patient with Down syndrome, an appropriate general approach includes:
options: Speaking only to family members present and never addressing the patient directly
Assuming the patient cannot participate at all in any decisions about their own care
Assuming all patients with Down syndrome have entirely identical needs and abilities
Communicating directly and respectfully with the patient, while involving caregivers as needed

q: When assessing a patient with cerebral palsy, the EMT should keep in mind that:
options: Baseline motor and speech patterns in cerebral palsy are similar enough across patients that a standard assessment approach is sufficient
Communication difficulties are common enough in cerebral palsy that verbal responses should generally be disregarded during assessment
Baseline muscle tone, movement patterns, or speech may differ from what's typical, so understanding the patient's normal baseline is valuable
Most patients with cerebral palsy show similar enough motor and speech patterns that a single standardized assessment approach applies broadly

q: When responding to a call involving a patient with a valid, applicable DNR (Do Not Resuscitate) order, the EMT should generally:
options: Follow local protocol regarding valid DNR orders, which generally means honoring properly documented, applicable orders while still providing comfort care
Refuse to respond to the call at all once dispatch mentions a possible DNR order is in place at the residence
Disregard any DNR paperwork that isn't the original document, since only an original signed copy is considered valid on scene
Perform full resuscitation until family members present at the scene can confirm the order is genuine

q: Elderly patients are more likely than younger patients to:
options: Take about the same number of medications as younger adults, since chronic conditions requiring multiple prescriptions are equally common across age groups
Metabolize medications the same way younger adults do, so standard adult dosing guidelines apply without adjustment
Take multiple medications (polypharmacy)
Experience medication-related complications about as often as younger adults, since drug metabolism doesn't meaningfully change with age

q: Regarding consent for a minor patient in a true emergency, EMS generally:
options: Requires the same written parental authorization form for a minor in a true emergency as for a routine, non-emergency call
Should wait for law enforcement to grant permission on the parent's behalf before treating an unaccompanied minor
Must locate and contact a parent or guardian by phone before beginning treatment, even in a life-threatening emergency
Can generally proceed under implied consent for genuine emergencies when a parent/guardian is not immediately available, per local protocol

q: A normal respiratory rate for a healthy newborn is generally around:
options: 100-120 breaths per minute
30-60 breaths per minute
4-8 breaths per minute
Respiratory rate does not apply to newborns

q: The Incident Command System (ICS) is used at emergency scenes primarily to:
options: Replace the need for any communication between agencies, since each agency independently manages its own personnel and objectives
Apply mainly to fire department operations, with law enforcement and EMS typically coordinating through their own separate command systems
Provide a standardized management structure for coordinating multiple responders/agencies
Determine which agency receives credit for the response, based on which unit arrived first and established initial scene control

q: "Unified command" in a multi-agency incident generally means:
options: Command rotates between agencies at set intervals throughout the incident to ensure fair representation
Representatives from multiple involved agencies jointly manage the incident using a shared set of objectives
The agency with primary legal jurisdiction takes sole charge, while other agencies operate under its direction
No command structure is used at all, since each responding unit operates independently based on its own judgment

q: A "rehab" sector established at a large-scale incident is generally intended to:
options: Provide a discharge location for patients who refuse transport after being cleared by an on-scene physician
Provide rest, rehydration, and medical monitoring for responders working the incident
Have no defined purpose, since responder fatigue and hydration are not considered scene safety concerns
