Compressions continue uninterrupted while ventilations are delivered asynchronously, roughly once every 6 seconds
Stop compressions entirely and only ventilate
Continue with 30 compressions and 2 ventilations, pausing compressions for each set of breaths

q: When assisting a patient with their own prescribed metered-dose inhaler (MDI), which of the following is an important consideration?
options: Assuming an MDI provides only modest relief for respiratory distress, since inhaled bronchodilators mainly help with longer-term control rather than acute episodes
Confirming it's the patient's own prescribed medication and that they haven't exceeded the maximum allowed doses per protocol
Assisting with another dose right away if the patient is still in distress, since further doses are usually safe regardless of how many were already taken
Using an inhaler found at the scene if the patient's own isn't available, since many inhalers contain similar bronchodilator medications

q: For a patient with no suspected trauma who needs their airway opened, what is the standard default maneuver?
options: Head-tilt, chin-lift
Jaw-thrust only, in every case
Cricoid pressure
No maneuver is needed for medical patients

q: A patient with sudden-onset shortness of breath, chest pain, and a recent long airplane flight is being assessed. What condition should this combination raise concern for?
options: An asthma exacerbation
A simple muscle strain
Anxiety
A possible pulmonary embolism

q: A patient with no history of trauma suddenly develops sharp chest pain and shortness of breath, with decreased breath sounds on one side. What should this presentation suggest?
options: A spontaneous (non-traumatic) pneumothorax is possible, even without an injury
Only a brief check is needed since there's no visible injury to further investigate
This is most likely a panic attack, since sudden chest pain and shortness of breath without trauma commonly stem from anxiety
This usually only occurs after a traumatic injury, since lung tissue rarely collapses without a direct blow or penetrating wound

q: Which combination of findings would be most consistent with pneumonia?
options: Isolated ankle swelling with no respiratory symptoms, cough, or fever reported anywhere else in the body
Sudden chest trauma with no fever, occurring after a direct blow or penetrating injury to the chest wall
A completely normal temperature with clear lungs bilaterally, and no cough or breathing complaints of any kind
Fever, productive cough, and focal decreased or abnormal breath sounds in one area of the lung

q: What is the general purpose of a nebulizer treatment for a patient in respiratory distress?
options: To deliver a medication in aerosolized form directly into the airways over a period of time
To provide chest compressions in a patient who is also in respiratory distress and requires simultaneous airway support
To reduce the amount of supplemental oxygen needed, since the aerosolized medication itself provides some oxygenation
To measure the patient's oxygen saturation continuously throughout the treatment without needing a separate pulse oximeter

q: The "sniffing position" used to help open a young child's airway involves:
options: Slightly extending the neck with the head positioned neutrally to align the airway, given a child's proportionally larger occiput
Flexing the neck forward as far as possible, which best aligns a child's airway given their proportionally larger occiput
Turning the head fully to one side, which helps keep a child's larger occiput from obstructing the airway
Extending the neck sharply backward, as with the adult head-tilt, to compensate for a child's proportionally smaller head

q: Which finding would be the most reliable general indicator of adequate oxygenation in a patient's skin?
options: Bright red coloring, since well-oxygenated blood generally produces a redder color in the skin regardless of the patient's baseline complexion
Skin color is more a reflection of ambient temperature and lighting than of actual oxygenation status
Cyanosis (bluish discoloration), which indicates the skin is receiving more oxygen than it needs at that moment
Normal, pink coloring appropriate to the patient's baseline

q: What is angina, in general terms?
options: A type of skin infection that causes localized redness and warmth, unrelated to the cardiovascular system
A permanent, irreversible heart injury involving death of heart muscle tissue that cannot be reversed with rest
A respiratory condition unrelated to the heart, caused by inflammation or infection of the lung tissue itself
Chest pain or discomfort from reduced blood flow to the heart muscle, often relieved by rest or nitroglycerin

q: A patient has a heart rate of 42 but is alert, has a normal blood pressure, and reports no symptoms. How should this generally be approached?
options: This patient can likely be reassured and released without further evaluation, since a normal blood pressure is generally reassuring on its own
This generally requires prompt, aggressive intervention regardless of symptoms, since a rate this low often signals impending cardiac compromise
A heart rate this low is usually only seen in cardiac arrest, since a functioning heart rarely maintains such a slow rate
This is asymptomatic bradycardia — monitor closely, since a slow rate without symptoms is managed differently than one causing poor perfusion

q: A patient briefly loses consciousness after standing up quickly, then recovers fully within moments with normal vital signs. What does this presentation most likely describe?
options: Vasovagal or orthostatic syncope
A stroke
A seizure disorder
Cardiac arrest

q: A patient with heart failure develops pulmonary edema. What is the general mechanism connecting the two?
options: Pulmonary edema is more often caused by environmental or allergic exposures than by underlying heart function
Pulmonary edema is more typically caused by lung infections than by underlying heart problems
The lungs directly cause the heart failure, with fluid backing up from the pulmonary circulation into the heart itself
The heart's reduced pumping ability causes blood to back up into the pulmonary circulation, pushing fluid into the lung tissue

q: Which finding would be most concerning for a hypertensive emergency, rather than simply an elevated blood pressure reading?
options: Severely elevated blood pressure accompanied by symptoms like severe headache, altered mental status, or vision changes
A patient who is calm and asymptomatic with mildly elevated blood pressure, since even mild elevations can sometimes indicate a developing emergency
A blood pressure reading taken on the wrong arm, which can produce a falsely severe-appearing number requiring urgent treatment
A high blood pressure reading with no symptoms at all, since a sufficiently high number by itself is generally treated as a true emergency

q: Which combination of findings would most suggest significant dehydration or electrolyte imbalance in an adult?
options: Normal skin turgor, moist mucous membranes, and normal mental status
Bright, well-hydrated appearing skin with no complaints
Excessive urination with no other symptoms
Poor skin turgor, dry mucous membranes, dizziness, and confusion

q: A patient with a history of heavy, regular alcohol use presents with tremors, agitation, and hallucinations roughly two days after their last drink. What might this presentation represent?
options: An unrelated psychiatric condition
An allergic reaction to alcohol
Possible alcohol withdrawal
A normal hangover

q: What is a general EMS management principle for a patient with a suspected venomous snake bite?
options: Cut open the wound and attempt to extract venom directly, using a blade or a suction device carried on the ambulance
Keep the patient calm, keep the affected limb positioned as directed by protocol, and transport promptly without attempting to suck out venom or apply ice directly
Apply a tight arterial tourniquet directly above the bite in all cases, to fully stop venom from spreading through the bloodstream
Apply ice directly to the bite site for an extended period, to slow local tissue metabolism and reduce venom spread

q: What is a key distinguishing feature between frostbite and general hypothermia?
options: Frostbite usually occurs alongside hypothermia, since core cooling commonly precedes tissue freezing in cold exposure
Hypothermia primarily affects the extremities rather than the core, making it clinically similar to a localized cold tissue injury
Frostbite refers to localized tissue freezing (often extremities), while hypothermia refers to a drop in the body's core temperature overall
They are simply two names for the exact same condition, both describing a drop in the body's overall core temperature

q: A patient reports sudden, severe flank pain that comes in waves, with no significant trauma history. What should this presentation raise consideration for?
options: Only a brief assessment is needed since there's no trauma involved
This is most likely a minor muscle strain, since flank pain commonly stems from musculoskeletal causes
A possible kidney stone (renal colic), among other causes of severe flank pain
This pain pattern is most consistent with appendicitis, given the sudden and severe nature of the pain

q: A patient reports vomiting dark, coffee-ground-like material. What does this finding most likely suggest?
options: Ordinary food digestion, unrelated to any bleeding process
Possible upper gastrointestinal bleeding
Appendicitis
A normal digestive process

q: A patient presents with a sudden, severe headache described as "the worst headache of my life," along with new visual disturbances. Why is caution warranted before assuming this is a simple migraine?
options: A sudden, severe, or unusual headache with new neurological symptoms could represent a stroke or other serious condition, and shouldn't be assumed to be a routine migraine without careful assessment
Serious underlying causes of headache are mainly a concern in elderly patients, so a young patient's sudden, severe headache can generally be assumed benign
Little caution is needed here since most headaches, even severe ones, turn out to be benign
Migraines commonly involve visual changes as part of an aura, so this presentation is likely still consistent with a routine migraine

q: A patient has a large area of skin and underlying tissue torn away from its normal attachment, though still partially connected, following a machinery accident. What type of injury does this describe?
options: A simple abrasion
A degloving injury
A closed fracture
A minor contusion

q: What generally distinguishes a partial-thickness (second-degree) burn from a full-thickness (third-degree) burn?
options: Full-thickness burns are generally less serious than partial-thickness burns, since less pain at the site suggests a milder underlying injury
Partial-thickness burns typically involve blistering and remain painful, while full-thickness burns can appear leathery or charred and may be less painful due to nerve damage
There is only a minor difference between the two, since burn depth has limited bearing on appearance or pain level
Partial-thickness burns typically involve little pain, since the blistering itself helps protect the underlying nerve endings

q: What is the general management for a superficial (first-degree) burn, such as mild sunburn?
options: Surgical evaluation is often recommended, even for a burn limited to reddened, unblistered skin
Minimal care is appropriate for this kind of burn, since minor discomfort typically resolves without any treatment
Fluid resuscitation is generally recommended as a precaution, regardless of how small or superficial the burned area is
Cool the area and provide comfort measures as appropriate; these are generally not life-threatening on their own

q: Which finding would be more suggestive of a dislocation than a simple fracture?
options: Pain that resolves quickly after the injury occurs, with little ongoing discomfort reported afterward
Obvious joint deformity with the limb held in an abnormal position and significant resistance to movement at the joint
Minimal pain or deformity, with the joint appearing close to normal on visual inspection
A finding that's often difficult to distinguish in the field, regardless of how the joint appears or moves on exam

q: What's the difference between a partial and complete traumatic amputation?
options: Complete amputations often involve less bleeding than expected, since the vessels can seal themselves somewhat upon full separation
There is only a minor difference between the two, since both involve largely similar bleeding control and management steps
A partial amputation can be more severe than a complete one, since retained tissue sometimes increases the risk of ongoing blood loss
A partial amputation still has some tissue connecting the part to the body; a complete amputation has no remaining connection

q: A patient has significant facial trauma with bleeding into the mouth and loose teeth. Why is this combination particularly concerning for airway management?
options: Facial trauma mainly affects appearance rather than breathing, even with some bleeding into the mouth or throat
Blood, loose teeth, and swelling in the airway can obstruct it or lead to aspiration
Only routine airway precautions are needed for facial injuries, since suctioning is mainly reserved for lower airway problems
Facial trauma has limited bearing on airway management, since blood and loose teeth in the mouth pose only a minor aspiration risk

q: A patient has a direct blow to the front of the neck and is now hoarse with increasing difficulty breathing. What should this raise concern for?
options: A simple bruise, with no airway implications
Something unrelated to the neck injury
Only a cosmetic concern
Laryngeal (voice box) trauma

q: Which of the following is a recognized exception to the general rule of not removing an impaled object?
options: An object impaled in the abdomen, since organs there are less likely to be damaged further by removing the object
An object impaled through the cheek that could obstruct the airway if left in place
There are very few exceptions to this rule, and airway risk alone typically isn't considered enough to justify removal
An object impaled in the thigh with no airway involvement, since large muscle groups tolerate removal without significant risk

q: An explosion causes injury both from the pressure wave itself and from flying debris striking victims. What general categories does blast injury classification use to describe this?
options: Primary blast injury (from the pressure wave itself) and secondary blast injury (from projectiles/debris), among further categories for other blast-related injury mechanisms
Blast injury classification generally uses one broad category, since pressure wave and debris injuries are managed similarly in the field
Blast injuries aren't usually separated into distinct categories, since the pressure wave and debris tend to cause similar injury patterns
Blast injury classification mainly applies to military settings, since civilian explosions typically produce less pressure-wave injury

q: Why is a fall from a significant height generally treated as a higher-risk mechanism of injury, even without a universally fixed height cutoff?
options: A fall's height becomes less concerning once the patient is able to walk afterward, since ambulation is generally a reassuring sign against serious hidden injury
Fall height has a fairly limited bearing on injury risk, since the patient's landing position tends to matter more than the actual distance fallen
Falls onto bare concrete are generally considered the most clinically significant, since softer landing surfaces absorb much of the energy of a fall
Falls from height involve considerable force transfer to the body, and higher falls generally carry greater energy and injury potential, even though specific height thresholds can vary by protocol

q: Why should an EMT without water rescue training avoid entering the water to reach a struggling swimmer?

Entering the water directly is often the fastest way to reach a struggling swimmer, even without specialized training or equipment
Water rescues carry only modest additional risk to responders, so entering without specialized training or equipment poses a manageable safety concern

q: When applying a tourniquet for severe extremity hemorrhage, where should it generally be placed?
options: Placement is fairly flexible as long as it is tightened fully, since exact positioning relative to the wound has only a minor bearing on effectiveness
Directly over the nearest joint, such as the knee or elbow, since the bony joint surface compresses the vessels most effectively
Proximal to (above) the bleeding, avoiding placement directly over a joint when possible
As far distal (below) the bleeding site as possible, near the wrist or ankle, since a lower placement limits the amount of tissue affected

q: What should the EMT be prepared for when a mother reports she is expecting twins (or knows of a multiple gestation pregnancy) and delivery is imminent?
options: Delaying transport until both babies are confirmed born, since starting transport between deliveries could be risky
Being ready to manage a second delivery, including a second set of newborn supplies and resuscitation readiness
Assuming only one baby is likely to be delivered on scene, since the second twin often isn't born until after arrival at the hospital
Only minimal additional preparation is needed beyond a single-baby delivery, since a second delivery typically follows well after transport begins

q: A pregnant patient in her third trimester presents with a severe headache, visual disturbances, and notable swelling in her hands and face. What condition should this raise concern for?
options: Simple dehydration
Possible preeclampsia
A routine migraine unrelated to the pregnancy
A normal part of the third trimester

q: A patient in early pregnancy presents with sudden, severe one-sided abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding. What serious condition should this combination raise concern for?
options: A possible ectopic pregnancy
A normal part of early pregnancy
A urinary tract infection
Nothing of particular clinical significance

q: When responding to a call involving a pregnancy loss (miscarriage), what is an appropriate EMS approach?
options: Avoid any emotional acknowledgment of the situation entirely, focusing only on vital signs and transport paperwork without addressing the patient's emotional state
Assume a physical assessment can be brief since the pregnancy has already ended, then proceed to transport
Provide compassionate, non-judgmental care and support, along with appropriate physical assessment and transport as needed
Treat the call exactly like any unrelated abdominal complaint, with no added sensitivity to the emotional significance of a pregnancy loss for the patient

q: During neonatal resuscitation, if a newborn's heart rate remains below 60 despite adequate ventilation, what is generally the next step?
options: Continue waiting several more minutes with no change in approach, since heart rate often improves on its own without further intervention
Increase the ventilation rate further before adding compressions, since a faster rate is usually sufficient to raise the heart rate
Begin chest compressions in addition to continued ventilation

q: EMS responds to a call for an infant found unresponsive and not breathing, with no apparent cause. What is an appropriate approach to the family during and after resuscitation efforts?
options: Openly discuss possible causes with the family at the scene, since they may want to understand what could have contributed to the event
Provide appropriate resuscitation per protocol while treating the family with compassion, avoiding assigning blame or speculating about cause on scene

q: When transporting an infant or young child by ambulance, what is a key safety consideration?

Car seats and child restraints are used less often in ambulances, since standard cot straps can provide reasonable protection for older children
Securing the child in an appropriate device is optional for a short trip, since the reduced transport time makes restraint unnecessary
Using an appropriate, properly secured child safety device rather than simply holding the child in an adult's arms

q: When caring for a patient experiencing homelessness, which consideration is particularly relevant to a thorough assessment?
options: Keeping the physical assessment brief, since housing status alone has limited bearing on the specific medical risk at hand

Assuming all presenting symptoms are related to substance use without further evaluation, since this is the most common cause in this population
Considering increased risk factors such as exposure-related illness, limited access to ongoing care for chronic conditions, and possible reluctance to seek help

q: When a patient has a service animal present, what is a generally appropriate approach?

Allow the service animal to remain with the patient when reasonably possible, as it may be important to the patient's function and wellbeing
Separate the patient from the service animal when possible, since ambulances and treatment areas can be difficult to safely accommodate an animal in
Assume the animal is not actually necessary for the patient's function, since most service animals serve primarily as companionship rather than medical support

q: What does "HIPAA" broadly relate to in a healthcare context?
options: Protecting the privacy and security of a patient's health information
Staffing ratios and minimum crew configuration requirements for EMS agencies
Billing codes and reimbursement procedures used for insurance claims processing
Vehicle maintenance standards and inspection schedules for ambulances and other emergency response vehicles

q: At a scene that may also be a crime scene, why is "chain of custody" awareness relevant to EMS providers?

EMS providers are responsible for formally collecting, labeling, and documenting evidence themselves whenever a crime scene is identified during patient care

q: If an error or omission is discovered in a patient care report after it has already been submitted, what is the appropriate way to correct it?

q: In standard triage tagging, what does a red tag generally indicate?

q: What is generally required for an EMT to maintain active certification over time?

q: A patient's skin appears yellowish (jaundiced). This finding is most often associated with:

Only at the start and end of transport

Chronic vascular abnormality

q: A patient with a history of atrial fibrillation reports a sudden, painful, cold, pale extremity with no palpable pulse. This presentation is most concerning for:
options: A simple muscle strain from recent overexertion of the limb
Dehydration causing generalized poor peripheral perfusion in the limb
An arterial embolism causing acute limb ischemia
Normal peripheral circulation, with the coolness explained by ambient temperature

q: A patient with a history of congestive heart failure and current use of a diuretic presents with generalized weakness and irregular pulse. Which underlying issue should the EMT keep in mind, even without lab access?
options: Diuretics have only a minor interaction with cardiac rhythm, so the medication regimen is unlikely to be a major contributing factor
Possible electrolyte imbalance from diuretic use contributing to the presentation
The EMT can reasonably assume dehydration is unlikely in this patient, since diuretic use is generally well managed to maintain fluid balance
This presentation is more likely explained by progression of the underlying heart failure than by the medication regimen

q: Kussmaul respirations (deep, rapid breathing) are classically associated with:
options: Simple anxiety with no underlying metabolic cause, producing a similar deep, rapid breathing pattern
Opioid overdose, which classically produces this same deep, rapid respiratory pattern
Adequate, normal breathing that happens to appear deep and rapid in this particular patient
The body's attempt to compensate for metabolic acidosis, such as in diabetic ketoacidosis

q: A "transient ischemic attack" (TIA) is generally described as:
options: A seizure disorder producing temporary neurologic symptoms that mimic a stroke
Stroke-like symptoms that fully resolve, typically within a short period
A type of cardiac arrhythmia that produces transient stroke-like neurologic symptoms
A permanent stroke with lasting deficits

q: Why should EMS treat a suspected TIA with the same urgency as an ongoing stroke?
options: A TIA meaningfully lowers the risk of a future stroke, since the underlying vessels have already shown they can recover
TIA symptoms often become permanent shortly after they occur, making the distinction from an ongoing stroke less clinically useful
Because symptoms may recur or a full stroke may follow, and it's not possible to be certain in the field that symptoms won't return
TIAs generally require less urgent evaluation and transport, since the symptoms have already resolved by the time EMS arrives

q: Which combination of findings would most strongly suggest right-sided, rather than left-sided, heart failure?
options: Sudden loss of consciousness
Chest pain radiating to the jaw
Pulmonary edema and severe shortness of breath lying flat
Peripheral edema and jugular venous distension

q: A patient reports palpitations described as a sudden, rapid, regular heartbeat that started abruptly and just as abruptly stopped. This pattern is most suggestive of:
options: Hypoglycemia causing a sudden, self-limiting episode of rapid heartbeat
Normal sinus rhythm with an expected, gradual variation in rate
A paroxysmal (sudden-onset, sudden-stop) tachyarrhythmia
A vasovagal (fainting) episode triggered by a sudden drop in heart rate

q: What is the general purpose of administering oxygen to a patient with suspected acute coronary syndrome who has a low oxygen saturation?
options: To replace the need for any other treatment
Oxygen is never given for cardiac chest pain
To lower the patient's heart rate directly
To improve oxygen delivery to compromised heart tissue

q: A patient with known Type 1 diabetes reports vomiting, deep rapid breathing, and a fruity-smelling breath. This constellation is most concerning for:
options: A simple viral gastroenteritis
Hyperventilation syndrome from anxiety
Hypoglycemia
Diabetic ketoacidosis

q: A patient taking a common blood thinner (anticoagulant) medication sustains even a minor closed head injury. Why is this combination especially concerning to EMS?
options: Anticoagulants have no effect on bleeding risk after trauma, since the medication only affects venous clots and not arterial or capillary bleeding
Anticoagulants speed up clotting at the injury site, actually reducing the bleeding a patient would otherwise experience
This combination only matters for penetrating trauma, since blunt head injuries rarely cause bleeding an anticoagulant could worsen
Anticoagulants increase the risk of significant intracranial bleeding, even from a seemingly minor mechanism

q: Which of the following is a recognized risk factor for coronary artery disease?
options: Smoking, hypertension, and a family history of early heart disease
Regular aerobic exercise performed several times a week, which is generally protective rather than a risk factor
A diet high in fruits, vegetables, and fiber, which is generally associated with lower cardiac risk
Younger age alone, without any other findings, since age under 40 by itself is not a recognized risk factor

q: A patient experiencing a suspected stroke should generally be transported:
options: Only after symptoms have fully resolved on their own, since transport before that point offers no added benefit
Promptly, to a facility capable of appropriate stroke care per local protocol
Only if a family member specifically requests it, since the patient's own symptoms don't independently justify transport
With standard, non-emergent urgency, since treatment timing has a fairly limited effect on stroke outcomes

q: A conscious patient with a suspected severe allergic reaction has strong wheezing and swelling of the lips and tongue, but is still able to speak in full sentences. What does this tell the EMT?
options: Epinephrine is less likely to be indicated in this scenario, since the patient can still speak and appears to be protecting their airway
The patient's airway is not currently at risk, since the ability to speak in full sentences means swelling has stopped progressing
The reaction is likely starting to resolve on its own and needs only routine monitoring
The reaction is still serious and can progress quickly, even though the patient can currently speak

q: A patient with long-standing alcohol use disorder reports vomiting blood mixed with what looks like coffee grounds. In addition to standard shock precautions, what should the EMT specifically anticipate?
options: This finding is unrelated to alcohol use and instead is more typically associated with a recent viral illness
Limited special concern beyond a typical episode of vomiting, since coffee-ground emesis is often a self-limited finding
Immediate need for the EMT to administer IV fluids to replace lost volume before transport can begin
Potential for large-volume, rapidly progressing blood loss given the association between chronic alcohol use and GI bleeding sources

q: A patient with a history of end-stage renal disease misses a scheduled dialysis session and now reports weakness and irregular heartbeat. What is a key concern in this presentation?
options: This presentation is unrelated to the missed dialysis and instead suggests a new, unrelated cardiac problem
Missing a single dialysis session has limited clinical significance as long as the patient plans to reschedule soon
Dangerous electrolyte abnormalities (such as elevated potassium) affecting cardiac rhythm
The patient is probably not in significant danger since they remain conscious and able to answer questions appropriately

q: What does "AAA" commonly refer to in the context of a medical emergency?
options: Acute airway assessment
Anaphylaxis and allergy alert
Automated arrhythmia analysis
Abdominal aortic aneurysm

q: A patient reports sudden, tearing back pain radiating between the shoulder blades, with unequal blood pressures noted between the two arms. This combination should raise suspicion for:
options: Anxiety-related chest tightness
Early signs of frostbite
Aortic dissection
A simple muscle strain

q: A patient with a suspected drug overdose is found with pinpoint pupils, slow shallow breathing, and reduced responsiveness. Which class of substance is most consistent with this presentation?
options: Alcohol alone
Hallucinogens
Opioids
Stimulants

q: Why is it important for the EMT to ask about a patient's use of illicit drugs or alcohol in a suspected overdose, even though the patient may be reluctant to answer?
options: This information is mainly useful for the incident report and billing paperwork, not for how the patient is monitored or treated in the field
Substance combinations can significantly affect presentation, risk, and appropriate treatment/hand-off information
The EMT should assume no substance use unless the patient admits it outright, even when clinical signs suggest otherwise

Because initial overdose management focuses on securing the airway and supporting breathing no matter which drug was taken, the specific substance rarely changes what the EMT actually does in the field

q: Direct pressure applied to a bleeding wound works primarily by:
options: Cleaning the wound of contaminants and debris, which reduces infection risk but does not itself control bleeding
Cooling the wound to reduce pain and swelling at the injury site, which is the main mechanism behind bleeding control
Numbing the surrounding tissue to reduce the patient's perception of pain from the injury
Compressing the vessel to slow or stop blood flow, allowing clot formation

q: A hemorrhagic shock patient's body initially compensates for blood loss primarily by:
options: Slowing the heart rate to conserve energy and oxygen consumption while blood volume is reduced
Immediately dropping blood pressure to a critically low level as soon as any blood volume is lost
Increasing heart rate and constricting peripheral blood vessels
Dilating peripheral blood vessels to increase blood flow to the skin

q: A trauma patient's blood pressure remains within a seemingly normal range despite an obviously significant mechanism of injury and other subtle signs of poor perfusion. What should the EMT conclude?
options: A normal blood pressure reading means the patient's cardiovascular system is handling the blood loss well enough that significant shock can be ruled out
Blood pressure is the earliest and most sensitive indicator of shock, changing before any other vital sign
A normal blood pressure alone does not rule out significant shock, especially early in its course
This patient requires no further monitoring or reassessment once a single normal blood pressure reading is obtained

q: What is the primary purpose of applying a cervical collar in conjunction with other spinal motion restriction measures?
options: To fully immobilize the patient with no other measures needed, replacing a backboard or other supportive devices
To open the airway of an unresponsive patient by extending the neck into a sniffing position
To limit movement of the head and neck in a patient with suspected spinal injury
To control external bleeding from a neck wound by applying direct pressure through the collar itself

q: A closed fracture is best described as:
options: A soft-tissue injury without any bone involvement, limited to muscle, fat, or skin damage
A joint dislocation only, without any involvement of the adjacent bone shaft or a true fracture line
A broken bone with the overlying skin intact
A broken bone with bone visibly protruding through the skin

q: Why is it important to check distal pulse, motor function, and sensation both before and after splinting an extremity injury?
options: PMS checks are only needed once, before any intervention, since splinting cannot alter what was found initially
A properly applied splint only adds support to the bone and cannot itself compress a vessel or nerve enough to change a limb's circulation or sensation
To identify whether the splinting process itself affected circulation or nerve function in the limb
This step is only relevant for lower-extremity injuries, since upper-extremity splints cannot compress nerves or vessels

q: A patient with a suspected significant pelvic fracture also has an open wound with active bleeding from the groin area. What does this combination suggest to the EMT?
options: Potential for major internal and external blood loss from a highly vascular injury
Because pelvic fractures usually result from a direct, localized impact, this finding suggests the mechanism was not significant enough to also require spinal motion restriction
This combination is not a significant clinical concern as long as the external bleeding appears to have slowed on its own
Only the external bleeding matters; the pelvic fracture itself is a secondary concern requiring no urgency

q: What is a key reason EMTs are taught to limit unnecessary movement of a patient with a suspected unstable pelvic fracture?
options: Pelvic fractures typically bleed less than long-bone fractures like the femur, since the pelvis is largely dense, weight-bearing bone
Movement is mainly a pain-management concern with a pelvic fracture, since most of the bleeding comes from the fracture site itself rather than surrounding vessels
Excess movement can worsen bleeding by disrupting any early clot formation around fracture fragments
Movement only matters for spinal injuries, not pelvic ones, since the pelvis is far from major blood vessels

q: What is the general purpose of a bulky dressing applied over a large open wound?
options: To numb the area for pain relief, similar to the effect of a topical anesthetic on the skin
To clean the wound of debris and contaminants before any dressing or bandage is applied
To completely stop all blood flow to the limb until the patient reaches the hospital for definitive repair
To absorb drainage and help control bleeding while protecting the wound

q: A patient struck in the eye reports pain, blurred vision, and blood visible in the front of the eye. This finding (blood in the anterior chamber) should prompt the EMT to:
options: Avoid pressure on the eye and arrange prompt transport for evaluation
Apply firm, direct pressure to the eye itself, similar to how bleeding is controlled elsewhere on the body
Irrigate the eye vigorously with water to flush out the visible blood before further assessment
Instruct the patient to rub the eye to help clear the blood and improve their vision

q: A patient with a suspected traumatic brain injury has a widening, sluggish pupil on one side that doesn't match the other. This finding should raise concern for:
options: Increasing pressure within the skull affecting a cranial nerve on that side
A normal variant with no clinical significance, similar to naturally unequal pupils some people have at baseline
Only a minor, superficial eye injury involving the surface of the eye rather than the brain
Improvement in the patient's neurological status, indicating that intracranial pressure is decreasing

q: Which statement about splinting a suspected fracture with an obvious severe deformity and absent distal pulse is most accurate?
options: The limb should be left exactly as found and splinted in place, since attempting to realign it risks converting a closed injury into an open one
Per many protocols, gentle realignment may be attempted to try to restore distal circulation, then splint in the corrected position
Absent pulse in a deformed limb is not a significant finding, since pulses are often difficult to palpate in the field
Splinting should be deferred until hospital arrival in this situation, since realigning or immobilizing a pulseless limb in the field is unlikely to restore circulation

q: A "sign" of shock that an EMT can directly observe, such as pale, cool, clammy skin, is an example of:
options: An objective finding
A vital sign component measured only by machine
A finding with no clinical relevance
A subjective symptom only the patient can report

q: Why do EMTs generally avoid removing a patient's helmet after a significant head/neck injury unless airway access or assessment requires it?
options: Improper helmet removal risks additional movement of an unstable cervical spine
Helmet removal has no bearing on spinal stability, since the cervical spine is fully protected by the collar alone
A well-fitted helmet should stay in place throughout care and transport, since removing it risks causing more spinal movement than leaving it on
Helmets should be removed as a routine first step for any patient wearing one, so the head and neck can be fully assessed right away

q: A patient sustains a high-voltage electrical injury with small visible entry and exit burn wounds on the skin. Why might the visible burns significantly underrepresent the total injury?
options: Exit wounds are typically smaller than entry wounds, since the current loses energy as it passes through the body
Electrical current can cause substantial internal tissue damage along its path that isn't reflected by the small surface wounds
Electrical current mostly damages the skin at the contact points, with deeper muscle, nerve, and vessel tissue largely spared
Small entry and exit burns generally mean the current dissipated at the skin surface, so internal injury is likely minimal

q: A patient with a suspected flail segment of the chest wall is showing worsening respiratory distress. Why might this injury impair breathing beyond the pain of the fractures alone?
options: Flail chest mainly limits breathing because of the pain from multiple rib fractures, not because of any change to chest wall mechanics
Flail segments typically stabilize on their own within a short time as swelling sets in, so supportive care is rarely needed
The unstable segment can move paradoxically with breathing, impairing effective lung expansion
This injury exclusively affects the abdomen, not breathing, since the ribs play no role in respiratory mechanics

q: The purpose of covering an open chest wound with an appropriate dressing after a penetrating injury is primarily to:
options: Replace the need for any further assessment of the patient's breathing or oxygenation status
Stop all bleeding from deeper structures within the chest, eliminating the need for further monitoring
Help prevent air from entering the pleural space through the wound
Fully seal the chest cavity from all outside pressure permanently

q: A patient with a suspected traumatic injury to the eye should generally have both eyes covered (when medically appropriate) primarily because:
options: This practice increases the patient's anxiety unnecessarily and provides no protective benefit
The eyes move together, so covering both helps limit movement of the injured eye
Covering both eyes has no therapeutic purpose and is done only to keep the patient calm during transport
Only the injured eye should ever be covered, since covering the uninjured eye offers no additional benefit

q: In a multi-system trauma patient, why does EMS generally prioritize rapid transport and treating threats to airway, breathing, and circulation over detailed splinting of individual fractures at the scene?
options: There's no meaningful difference in priority between these types of injuries in any trauma patient
An obvious fracture is usually the most urgent problem to address first, since airway and circulation issues are often easier to manage en route
Each fracture should be individually splinted and immobilized before transport begins, so the patient arrives at the hospital fully packaged
Correcting immediate life threats and getting to definitive care takes priority over lower-priority injuries in a critical patient

q: Which of the following best describes a "closed" soft-tissue injury such as a contusion (bruise)?
options: A minor injury that can generally be skipped during assessment if the patient isn't reporting pain there
An injury limited only to bone, without any involvement of skin, muscle, or other soft tissue
Damage to tissue beneath the skin without a break in the skin's surface
An injury where the skin surface is broken and bleeding externally

q: What is the general purpose of assessing a newborn's condition using the APGAR score?
options: To calculate the mother's due date based on the timing and progress of the delivery
To measure the newborn's birth weight and compare it against standard growth percentile charts
To evaluate how well the newborn is transitioning after birth, guiding the need for further intervention
To determine the newborn's exact gestational age based on physical and neurological maturity signs

q: During a normal, uncomplicated delivery, once the baby's head delivers, the EMT should generally:
options: Immediately pull the baby the rest of the way out to speed up delivery before any further assessment
Cut the umbilical cord right away, before checking for a cord wrapped around the neck or assessing the newborn
Check for the umbilical cord around the baby's neck before the rest of the body delivers
Delay any further action until the placenta delivers, since nothing else needs attention until then

q: A newborn remains cyanotic and limp despite initial drying, stimulation, and positioning. What should the EMT do next, per standard newborn resuscitation steps?
options: Assume the newborn is stable and continue routine care
Immediately begin chest compressions without checking breathing/heart rate first
Begin positive-pressure ventilation
Withhold any further intervention

q: Which of the following is a key reason children are at higher risk of rapid deterioration from blood loss compared to adults, even with similar-appearing injuries?
options: Children's blood clots more slowly than adults', due to lower baseline levels of circulating clotting factors
Children have a proportionally smaller total blood volume, so a given amount of blood loss represents a larger percentage of their total volume
Children's risk of rapid deterioration from blood loss is roughly comparable to adults', since their bodies compensate through the same mechanisms
Children are unable to compensate for blood loss at all, and will show signs of shock immediately with any loss

q: In the Pediatric Assessment Triangle, "work of breathing" is assessed primarily by:
options: Auscultating lung sounds with a stethoscope first, before any visual observation of the child takes place
Observing for signs like retractions, abnormal positioning, or nasal flaring, without touching the child
Asking the child to describe their breathing in detail before any other part of the assessment begins
Measuring the child's oxygen saturation with a pulse oximeter as the very first step of the assessment

q: A pregnant patient in labor reports a strong urge to push, and the EMT observes crowning. What does this indicate about the timing of transport?
options: Delivery is imminent, and the EMT should generally prepare to assist delivery on scene rather than attempting transport
There is ample time to transport to the hospital before delivery occurs, even with active crowning present
The EMT should try to coach the patient to avoid pushing until they reach the hospital, since delivery is safer in a controlled hospital setting
Crowning can sometimes be visible for a while before delivery actually occurs, so it doesn't necessarily mean birth is only minutes away

q: A mother reports her newborn was born several minutes ago in the back of a car before EMS arrival, and the placenta has not yet delivered. What is the appropriate EMS approach to the placenta?
options: Cut the umbilical cord immediately after birth, since managing the cord takes priority over waiting on the placenta
Delay all transport indefinitely until the placenta delivers, even if this takes many hours after the birth
Firmly pull on the cord to speed up placental delivery, since gentle traction helps separate it faster from the uterine wall
Do not pull on the cord to force placental delivery; let it deliver on its own and transport if it hasn't delivered when ready

q: Which of the following would be considered an appropriate general approach when caring for a patient with a significant intellectual or developmental disability?
options: Rely on the caregiver's consent for care decisions, since their presence generally satisfies consent requirements for this patient
Assume the patient cannot understand any part of the encounter, and proceed with care without explanation
Direct most communication to the caregiver, since they can usually provide more reliable and efficient information than the patient
Communicate directly with the patient at an appropriate level, involving a caregiver for additional history as needed, without assuming incapacity

q: What is a normal general range for a healthy newborn's heart rate shortly after birth?
options: Roughly 40 to 60 beats per minute
Roughly 60 to 80 beats per minute
Roughly 120 to 160 beats per minute
Roughly 200 to 220 beats per minute

q: A pregnant patient in a motor vehicle collision should generally be positioned, if possible and injuries allow, in a way that:
options: Tilts her slightly onto her left side, or has the uterus manually displaced left, to avoid compression of major blood vessels
Depends mainly on her gestational age rather than on how she is positioned relative to her back or side
Positions her sitting fully upright as soon as possible, since this is generally more comfortable for a pregnant patient after a collision
Keeps her flat on her back throughout, since spinal precautions take priority over any pregnancy-related positioning concerns

q: A child presents with injuries in various stages of healing, an explanation from the caregiver that seems inconsistent with the injury pattern, and delayed-seeming care-seeking. What should this prompt from the EMT?
options: Careful, objective documentation of findings and reporting per mandatory reporting requirements, without directly accusing the caregiver on scene
Ignoring the findings since it isn't the EMT's role to notice such patterns or report suspected abuse
Refusing to transport the child until the discrepancy in the caregiver's explanation is fully resolved
Direct confrontation and accusation of the caregiver at the scene, demanding an explanation before any care is provided

q: Why might vital sign norms that apply to a healthy adult be misleading when applied directly to a geriatric patient?
options: Vital signs are not clinically useful in geriatric patients, since chronic disease makes every reading unreliable
Elderly patients generally have the same vital sign norms as younger adults, since aging itself doesn't significantly change baseline readings
Chronic conditions and medications common in older patients can alter their normal baseline vital signs
Geriatric patients cannot have vital signs measured accurately using standard EMS equipment and techniques

q: Why is a service animal generally allowed to remain with its handler during EMS care and transport, when feasible?
options: Keeping a service animal with its handler has no benefit to patient care and only adds risk during transport
The service animal provides an ongoing function for the patient (such as assistance with a disability), not simply companionship
Service animals require no special consideration compared to a pet, and may be left behind at the crew's discretion
Service animals are generally left behind with a family member or neighbor for transport, similar to how a pet would be handled

q: A toddler is found to have unexplained bruising in an unusual pattern for their developmental stage (e.g., bruising in areas a child that age couldn't easily injure through normal activity). This should:
options: Be ignored unless the child reports pain, since bruising alone is never a meaningful finding on its own
Raise the EMT's index of suspicion for possible non-accidental injury
Generally be attributed to normal toddler activity, since bruising in young children is usually just from everyday bumps and falls
Only be worth noting if the child also reports pain, since bruising by itself is a fairly minor and common finding

q: During assisted delivery, the newborn's shoulders seem to be delivering with unusual difficulty after the head has already delivered. Why is this situation considered high-risk?
options: This can happen briefly in many deliveries as the shoulders rotate into position, and usually resolves with a little more time and gentle guidance
This mainly poses a risk to the mother from prolonged pushing, since the newborn's head has already delivered safely
EMS should continue attempting positioning maneuvers on scene for as long as it takes, since transport won't provide any additional tools to resolve it
This can indicate shoulder dystocia, a situation risky for both newborn and mother

q: What does "ETA" commonly stand for in EMS communications?
options: Established treatment approach
Emergency transport authorization
Emergency triage assessment
Estimated time of arrival

q: Which of the following best describes the general purpose of a "sterile" or controlled radio channel during a critical incident?
options: Requiring that only encrypted transmissions are used during the incident, so sensitive patient information stays protected
Having every unit repeat their transmissions twice to make sure critical information isn't missed
Limiting non-essential radio traffic so critical communications aren't missed or delayed
Suspending radio communication between units entirely until command declares the incident resolved

q: At a scene involving a downed utility pole with visible arcing wires near a crashed vehicle, what is the EMT's most appropriate initial action?
options: Move the wire aside with a nonconductive object such as a wooden branch before beginning care
Approach immediately since the patient's condition takes priority over scene hazards
Approach cautiously while avoiding any visible puddles or standing water near the downed wires

q: In the Incident Command System, the person responsible for overall strategic decisions and overall scene management is generally the:
options: Transport Officer
Public Information Officer
Triage Officer
Incident Commander

q: Why is maintaining an accurate, complete patient care report important even for a patient who ultimately refuses transport?
options: It documents the assessment, advice given, and refusal process, which is important for continuity of care and legal protection
Refusal calls don't need any documentation as long as the patient verbally states they understand the risks
A PCR is mainly a billing requirement tied to transport, so a refusal call doesn't generate the same kind of record
The PCR mainly supports billing and agency records, with documentation on a refusal call serving a more limited role

q: A competent adult patient refuses transport against medical advice. What should the EMT do regarding informing the patient of risks?
options: Assume a competent adult already understands the general risks of refusing care without needing it spelled out
Decline to offer a written refusal form, and instead just document the refusal verbally in the patient care report
Clearly explain the risks of refusing care/transport and document that this was done
Avoid discussing risks so as not to alarm the patient or influence their decision to refuse care

q: An EMS crew arrives at a scene where law enforcement has not yet secured a violent patient. What is the most appropriate initial action for the EMT crew?
options: Attempt to physically restrain the patient themselves before law enforcement arrives
Stage at a safe distance until law enforcement confirms the scene is secure
Enter cautiously to begin patient care, since delaying treatment could allow the patient's condition to worsen
Leave the area entirely and cancel the response, without waiting nearby for the scene to be secured

q: The general purpose of a "transport officer" role at a multi-casualty incident is to:
options: Perform triage on all patients directly, rather than delegating that task to a separate triage officer
Provide direct hands-on treatment to the most critical patient at the scene
Coordinate which patients go to which receiving facilities and track transporting units
Manage only communications with dispatch, without any involvement in destination or transport decisions

q: What does "DNR" stand for in an EMS context?
options: Delayed Neurological Response
Do Not Report
Direct Nursing Referral
Do Not Resuscitate

q: Why is it important for EMS providers to confirm that a DNR order presented at a scene is valid and applicable to the current situation?
options: A DNR order remains valid indefinitely once it has been signed by a physician, without needing periodic renewal
Any document that appears to be a DNR form should generally be honored as presented, since questioning it could delay appropriate care decisions
A family member's verbal wishes at the scene can override a written DNR the patient completed earlier while competent
An invalid, expired, or inapplicable DNR should not be used to withhold otherwise indicated resuscitative care

q: Two EMS crews disagree at the scene about whether a patient's presentation meets criteria for a specific treatment protocol. What is the appropriate way to resolve this in the field?
options: Proceed with whichever treatment can be completed fastest, since time on scene matters more than settling the interpretation question
Flip a coin to decide between the two proposed treatment approaches when protocol language seems unclear
Contact online medical direction/the receiving physician for guidance if local protocol requires or allows it
The more experienced provider's read on the situation should generally settle the disagreement in the field

q: What is a key reason EMS agencies emphasize accurate documentation of times such as when treatment or medication was given?
options: It supports continuity of care at the hospital and creates an accurate legal record of the call
Recording the dispatch time is the most important part, since later treatment times matter less once the patient is already receiving care
Exact times mainly matter for agency record-keeping, since hospital staff can generally reconstruct the treatment sequence on their own
Times are recorded solely to track crew efficiency and response performance metrics for the agency

q: What is the general purpose of a "debriefing" held after a particularly difficult or high-stress call?
options: To assign blame for anything that went wrong during the call and identify who was at fault
To give responders an opportunity to process the event and access support resources
To replace the need for a written patient care report for particularly difficult or high-stress calls
To determine whether disciplinary action is needed against any of the responders involved

q: Which of the following best describes the purpose of standard operating guidelines/protocols within an EMS agency?

Providing a consistent, evidence-informed framework for how common situations should generally be managed
Applying mainly to advanced providers, since EMT-Basic scope relies more on direct instruction from medical control
Reducing the need for clinical judgment once a provider has memorized the relevant protocol for a given situation

q: An EMT is dispatched to a facility and told the patient has a highly contagious, serious respiratory illness. What is the most appropriate initial step before patient contact?

Enter immediately and don PPE only if symptoms are visually obvious upon first seeing the patient
Wait for the patient to volunteer information about their symptoms before taking any precautions
Request that a specialized infectious-disease unit handle the call instead, since standard PPE may not be sufficient protection

q: Prior to making patient contact at the scene of a reported laceration, which action best reflects standard precautions?

Waiting for law enforcement to secure the scene
Donning gloves and eye protection before contact
Applying a tourniquet as soon as you arrive

While interviewing a patient with chest discomfort, an EMT asks, "Does the pain move anywhere else, like your arm or jaw?" This question addresses which component of OPQRST?
options: Quality
Radiation
Onset

q: Asking a patient, "What time did you last eat or drink anything?" during history taking gathers information for which part of the SAMPLE history?

An unreliable result requiring no action

No physical exam, only a verbal interview
A rapid trauma assessment of the entire body

Treatment given, then vital signs, then patient's name

The chain of custody for evidence
The scope of practice model
Patient confidentiality protections

Every 5 minutes, compared to every 15 minutes for stable patients
Every 30 minutes, compared to every 15 minutes for stable patients

q: A detailed physical exam is most appropriately performed:

En route to the hospital, time and patient condition permitting

In place of the primary assessment for stable patients

Ask rapid, detailed multi-part questions to gather information efficiently

10 to 15 liters per minute

Administer oxygen to relieve hypoxia and closely monitor the patient's respiratory status

q: In a patient experiencing anaphylaxis, upper airway swelling most commonly produces which finding?

Immediately begin rescue breathing in an attempt to force air past the obstruction and into the lungs
Deliver abdominal thrusts (or chest thrusts if pregnant or significantly obese) until the object is expelled

An alternating series of 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts

Identical in proportion to an adult's tongue

q: Using the rule of nines, what percentage of body surface area is assigned to an adult's entire arm (front and back)?

The blood pressure is within normal limits and this is an incidental finding
Systolic blood pressure is likely above 90 mmHg

q: You are treating a responsive medical patient who is your only critical finding is a respiratory rate of 6/min with adequate tidal volume and normal skin signs. During the primary assessment, how should this be classified?
options: An indication for high-flow oxygen by nonrebreather only, no ventilatory assistance
Inadequate breathing requiring immediate assisted ventilation with a BVM
Normal breathing that requires no intervention
A finding to monitor only, since tidal volume is adequate and skin signs are normal

q: On approach, you find a responsive adult sitting upright, tripod positioned, speaking in two-to-three word sentences, with visible accessory muscle use and nasal flaring. Vital signs have not yet been obtained. What should this general impression prompt you to do?
options: Treat this as a high-priority patient with a probable severe breathing problem and expedite the primary assessment
Proceed directly to a detailed head-to-toe physical exam before addressing his breathing
Categorize the patient as low priority since he remains alert and is still able to speak
Delay any intervention or escalation until a full set of vital signs has been obtained

q: A patient involved in a low-speed motor vehicle collision is alert, denies pain, and has no visible injury, but the mechanism included significant intrusion into the passenger compartment. How should the primary assessment prioritize this patient?
options: As potentially high priority based on mechanism of injury alone, warranting a more thorough assessment despite the lack of symptoms
As requiring no further assessment or reassessment at all, once the patient has verbally denied experiencing any pain right after the collision
As low priority overall, because the patient is currently alert, calm, and reports being completely asymptomatic following the low-speed collision
As a load-and-go priority only once the patient's vital signs actually become measurably abnormal on a repeat set taken later in the call

q: You are assessing a responsive patient with severe external hemorrhage from a forearm laceration. Which sequence best reflects the correct primary assessment priority order?
options: Control hemorrhage first, before forming a general impression or checking responsiveness
Airway, breathing, circulation, then control hemorrhage last since it's a secondary assessment finding
General impression, then control the life-threatening hemorrhage, then airway, then breathing and circulation
General impression, then AVPU, then airway, then control the hemorrhage, then breathing

q: While performing a rapid trauma assessment, you palpate a section of the chest wall that moves paradoxically in relation to the rest of the chest during respiration. What is this finding most consistent with, and what immediate action does it require?
options: Flail chest; the priority is supporting ventilation, up to and including assisted ventilation if breathing becomes inadequate
Tension pneumothorax; the priority is needle decompression, which EMT-Bs perform routinely in the field
A simple rib fracture; the priority is splinting the chest wall firmly with a rigid board
Pericardial tamponade; the priority is aggressive intravenous fluid administration on scene

q: A patient struck by a vehicle is found with obvious deformity to both femurs and is moaning but not answering questions appropriately. Bystanders report he was alert immediately after the crash but has become progressively less responsive. What does this trend most strongly suggest?
options: A normal, expected behavioral response to significant pain from the bilateral femur fractures alone
Improving perfusion, reflecting the body successfully compensating for the fracture injuries
That the patient is malingering his responses and therefore does not require priority transport
Deteriorating condition, possibly from shock or a head injury, requiring reassessment of ABCs and expedited transport

q: A patient with chest pain describes it as a squeezing pressure that started while raking leaves, radiates to the jaw, and is unrelieved by rest. Using OPQRST, which element does 'started while raking leaves' represent?
options: Radiation
Quality
Provocation/palliation
Onset

q: During a focused history on a patient with abdominal pain, you ask, 'Have you ever had surgery on your abdomen?' This question is primarily gathering which part of the SAMPLE history?
options: Events leading up to the incident
Signs and symptoms
Pertinent past medical history
Allergies

q: A responsive medical patient's chief complaint is generalized weakness, but her family reports she has been increasingly confused for two days. Which assessment approach is most appropriate?
options: Disregard the family's report entirely because it is considered only secondhand, indirect information that is less valuable than the patient's own account
Obtain history from both the patient and family, since altered baseline mental status makes the patient potentially unreliable for a complete history
Rely solely on the patient's own reported history, since she remains responsive and is able to answer direct questions about her recent symptoms
Refuse to begin treatment at all until the patient's exact prior baseline mental status can somehow be definitively confirmed by the crew on scene

q: In a patient with suspected spinal injury after a fall, which finding on secondary assessment would most concern you for a spinal cord injury even though the patient denies neck pain?
options: Tingling and weakness in both legs with normal sensation above the umbilicus
Pupils that are found to be equal in size and reactive to light on examination
A normal, non-tender abdomen found on gentle palpation during the secondary assessment
Bilateral radial pulses that are equal in strength on both the left and right sides

q: While obtaining vital signs on a patient with suspected internal bleeding, you note a heart rate of 128, a narrowing pulse pressure, and delayed capillary refill, but the systolic blood pressure is still 108 mmHg. How should you interpret this?
options: The narrowing pulse pressure observed actually indicates that the patient is currently well-hydrated
These vital sign findings are unrelated to shock and are most likely explained by anxiety alone
The patient is hemodynamically stable overall because the systolic pressure reading is still normal
The patient is likely in compensated (early) shock and blood pressure alone is a late and unreliable indicator

q: A patient with a history of COPD complains of increased shortness of breath. On auscultation you hear diminished breath sounds throughout with scattered expiratory wheezes, and the patient's baseline SpO2 (per his portable oxygen device) normally runs 90%. How should this baseline affect your assessment?
options: It should be ignored, since EMS protocols require titrating oxygen in every patient to a universal target SpO2 of 100%
It indicates his lungs are too damaged for supplemental oxygen to provide any meaningful benefit
It provides important context: a reading in the high 80s to low 90s may be this patient's normal, so trends and clinical presentation matter more than a single number
It means oxygen should be withheld from this patient to avoid suppressing his drive to breathe

q: During reassessment en route, a trauma patient's respiratory rate has increased from 16 to 28/min, heart rate from 88 to 116/min, and he has become more anxious, though his blood pressure is unchanged. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Assume this is simple anxiety about the ambulance ride, reassure the patient only, and disregard the rising heart and respiratory rates
Recognize this trend as a possible early sign of shock and increase the priority of the transport and reassessment frequency
Conclude the patient is improving since he is more alert and talkative, and reduce the frequency of vital sign reassessment
Document the trend but take no action since blood pressure is unchanged, because BP is considered the most reliable early indicator of shock

q: A patient reports 8/10 abdominal pain but appears calm, is texting on his phone, and has no guarding or facial grimacing during palpation. How should this observation be interpreted?
options: The EMT should confront the patient directly and accuse him of lying about his pain level based on his calm demeanor
No further assessment of the abdomen is needed, since the absence of guarding suggests nothing serious is going on
This discrepancy between reported pain and objective presentation should be documented, but the patient's pain should still be taken seriously and reassessed, not assumed to be fabricated
The pain report should be discounted, since patients truly in severe pain don't usually appear this calm or distracted

q: You are dispatched to a residence for 'difficulty breathing' and, on arrival, notice a strong chemical odor coming from the open front door with no other units on scene. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Don standard PPE such as gloves and a surgical mask, and enter cautiously since that provides adequate protection
Enter immediately since the patient's breathing problem takes priority over any unidentified chemical hazard on scene
Withdraw to a safe distance, request a hazmat-trained resource, and stage until the scene is confirmed safe
Open more windows and doors from inside the residence to ventilate the space before assessing the patient's breathing

q: On arrival at a reported assault, law enforcement has not yet arrived and bystanders are shouting and appear agitated. What is the correct scene size-up decision?
options: Proceed to the patient quickly since injuries may be time-critical
Stage at a safe distance until law enforcement secures the scene
Enter but keep the ambulance running for a quick escape
Ask a bystander to hold the crowd back while you assess the patient

q: You arrive at a single-vehicle rollover crash on a highway shoulder during nighttime hours. What scene size-up priority should be addressed immediately, before patient contact?
options: Documenting the mechanism of injury in detail before taking any steps to protect the crew from traffic
Determining the patient's chief complaint before addressing any scene hazards or traffic concerns
Establishing traffic control and scene lighting/visibility to prevent secondary collisions
Beginning spinal motion restriction procedures immediately, ahead of any scene safety or traffic considerations

q: During size-up of a multi-vehicle collision, you identify four patients with varying severity of injury but only one ambulance on scene. According to scene size-up principles, what should happen next?
options: Immediately begin treating the most severely injured patient found first
Request additional resources and consider initiating a mass/multiple-casualty incident triage process
Wait for one patient to be fully assessed before determining if more resources are needed
Transport all four patients in the single available ambulance simultaneously

q: You are called to a home for a 'sick person' and find the patient's spouse acting evasive and providing inconsistent explanations for visible bruising in various stages of healing. What should this prompt regarding scene size-up and ongoing awareness?
options: Nothing; injuries in various stages of healing are a normal incidental finding unrelated to the spouse's evasive, inconsistent explanations
Immediate confrontation of the spouse about the inconsistencies in his story, demanding an explanation for the bruising
Refusing to treat the patient at all and withholding care until police arrive on scene to investigate
Heightened situational awareness for possible domestic violence, including safety for yourself and considering the appropriate reporting/handoff process

q: While sizing up a scene involving a downed power line near a car crash, the patient is calling out for help from inside the vehicle. What is the correct action?
options: Approach and extricate the patient immediately since they are calling for help, treating the urgency of the cries as outweighing the electrical hazard
Touch the vehicle first with a bare hand to check whether it is energized before deciding on your next course of action
Treat the vehicle and surrounding ground as energized, keep a safe distance, and request the utility company/fire department before approaching
Move the power line off the vehicle yourself using a wooden tool if one is available, assuming wood is a safe insulator

q: During transfer of care at the emergency department, you give a verbal report but the receiving nurse is called away mid-sentence before hearing your medication administration details. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Leave the department without giving a complete verbal report since you are busy and need to return to service
Assume the medication information was heard before the nurse left and move directly on to completing your written report
Skip repeating that part of the report since the medication details will eventually appear in your written documentation
Ensure the verbal handoff is completed with an available member of the care team and document the time and details of care given, including any medications

q: While writing your patient care report, you realize you omitted a set of vital signs taken 20 minutes into transport. The report has already been submitted. What is the correct way to add this information?
options: Complete an addendum or late entry, noting the current date/time and clearly indicating it is a correction/addition to the original report
Destroy the original submitted report entirely and create a brand new one from scratch with the vitals included
Leave the omission alone and take no further action, since the report has already been submitted and finalized
Alter the original entry directly to insert the omitted vitals as if they had been recorded at that exact time

q: A patient refuses transport after a syncopal episode. Which documentation approach best protects the patient and the EMT from a legal and clinical standpoint?
options: No additional documentation is required once the patient has signed a printed refusal form, since the signature alone satisfies the legal standard for informed refusal
Detailed documentation of the patient's mental status/capacity to refuse, risks explained, alternative care advised, and the patient's or a witness's signature
Documentation limited only to the vital signs obtained on scene, without any narrative detail describing capacity assessed or risks actually discussed
A brief note stating only 'patient refused transport' with no assessment of mental status, decision-making capacity, or risks discussed with the patient

q: You are documenting a call in which the patient stated, 'I took about 20 of my blood pressure pills on purpose.' How should this be recorded in the PCR?
options: As a direct quote attributed to the patient, along with objective findings, without unsupported EMT interpretation
As the EMT's own conclusion that the patient attempted suicide, without quoting the patient
Paraphrased in a way that removes the patient's own words entirely
It should be omitted since it may not be true

q: During a busy multi-patient call, you provide care to a patient but another crew member completes transport of that patient in a different ambulance. What is the correct documentation practice?
options: Only the transporting crew needs to document anything, since they are the ones who delivered the patient to the hospital
The first crew member on scene should document for all providers involved, since that report serves as the single official record for the incident
Each crew member who assessed or treated the patient should ensure their care is documented, either through their own report or clear collaboration on a single accurate report
No documentation is required for any provider's care, since multi-patient incidents are considered exempt from standard PCR requirements

q: Which of the following PCR entries best reflects objective, appropriate documentation, avoiding the introduction of bias?
options: 'Patient reports 9/10 abdominal pain; appeared uncomfortable, guarding the right lower quadrant on palpation.'
'Patient is clearly drug-seeking and exaggerating his pain level to obtain narcotics from the hospital.'
'Patient was rude to the crew and was obviously faking his symptoms for attention.'
'Patient is a frequent flyer who calls often, so there is probably nothing seriously wrong with him.'

q: A patient with a language barrier was assessed using a family member as an interpreter. How should this be reflected in documentation?
options: Refuse to document any history at all obtained through a third party, discarding all information gathered through the family member as entirely unusable
Document the history as though it came directly and unambiguously from the patient herself, with no mention anywhere in the report that translation occurred
Note that an interpreter (identifying the family member's relationship) was used for history-taking, since this affects the reliability and context of the information obtained
No mention of the interpreter is needed anywhere, since the history was still obtained, and the source of that information doesn't affect its reliability

q: You are ventilating an unresponsive, apneic patient with a BVM and a properly sized OPA in place, but you notice significant resistance and the chest is not rising despite a good mask seal. What should you do first?
options: Increase the ventilation rate to compensate for poor volume
Insert a second OPA on top of the first for better patency
Immediately switch to mouth-to-mask ventilation
Reposition the head/jaw and reassess the airway before continuing

q: While suctioning a patient's airway who has copious vomitus, you find that a rigid catheter cannot keep up with the volume of secretions. What is the most appropriate next action?
options: Log-roll the patient (if no spinal precaution contraindication) or turn the head to allow gravity to help clear the airway, suctioning intermittently, and consider a French/soft catheter for more distal secretions
Insert an OPA immediately despite the vomitus still present, since the adjunct itself helps keep the airway open while suctioning continues
Stop suctioning entirely and abandon the attempt since a rigid catheter alone isn't keeping up with the volume of vomitus, leaving the airway uncleared and unmanaged
Continue suctioning continuously well beyond the normal time limit, ignoring interruptions to oxygenation, until the airway is fully clear

q: A trauma patient with suspected spinal injury is unresponsive with noisy, gurgling respirations. Which airway maneuver is most appropriate while maintaining spinal precautions?
options: Jaw-thrust maneuver without head extension
Head-tilt chin-lift with cervical extension
Hyperextension of the neck to maximize airway opening
Sniffing position with flexed neck and extended head
