Begin full resuscitation efforts including CPR and AED, since every patient found without signs of life should receive attempted resuscitation until a physician pronounces death
Recognize this as an obvious sign of death, and per most protocols, resuscitation efforts are not initiated; focus shifts to scene preservation and appropriate notifications

q: A trauma patient meets criteria for spinal motion restriction after a fall, but also has severe respiratory distress requiring repositioning to a seated position to breathe adequately. How should these competing priorities be managed?
options: Refuse to treat either problem until the patient can be fully supine and immobilized, since attempting airway management in a non-standard position risks worsening the spinal injury

Airway and breathing take priority over spinal motion restriction; the patient can be positioned to optimize breathing while using manual stabilization and modified techniques to minimize spinal movement as much as possible
Always prioritize full spinal immobilization over airway/breathing management, since preventing further spinal cord damage takes precedence over any degree of respiratory distress
Withhold oxygen until spinal precautions are fully completed, since supplemental oxygen delivered before immobilization is finished could encourage unnecessary patient movement

q: You arrive at a scene where a patient was struck by lightning and is now in cardiac arrest, along with a second patient nearby who is conscious but confused. In contrast to normal multiple-casualty triage, why might the arrested patient be prioritized for resuscitation here?
options: The confused, conscious patient should always be prioritized instead in any multi-patient scene like this one, since standard triage principles dictate that any patient in cardiac arrest is automatically the lowest priority

Cardiac arrest from lightning strike is often due to a temporary asystolic 'stunning' of the heart, and prompt CPR/AED can lead to good outcomes since these patients otherwise may have relatively few other traumatic injuries — an exception to the usual triage approach of deprioritizing arrest victims in multi-patient scenes

Lightning strike patients should never receive any resuscitation efforts at all, since the massive electrical current involved always causes immediately and universally fatal injuries to every organ system
Both patients should be treated with identical priority in this case, since triage categories do not meaningfully differentiate between a patient in full arrest and one who is simply confused

q: A patient with a suspected traumatic amputation of a finger has both the injury site and the amputated part available. What is the correct care for the amputated part during transport?
options: Discard the amputated part since reattachment is never possible in the field or hospital, so transporting the part along with the patient serves no useful purpose
Submerge the amputated part directly in water for transport, since keeping the tissue immersed prevents it from drying out during the trip to the hospital
Place the amputated part directly on ice with no protective wrapping, since direct contact with ice cools the tissue fastest and best preserves it for possible reattachment

Wrap the part in sterile gauze (moistened per protocol), place it in a sealed plastic bag, and keep that bag cool by placing it on ice (not directly submerged in ice or water) for transport with the patient

q: An elderly patient with a fall has minimal visible bruising but takes a blood-thinning medication daily. Why should this history significantly raise concern for internal injury, particularly intracranial bleeding, even with a seemingly minor fall?
options: This history means the patient should not be transported since nothing can be done, as there are no hospital-based treatments capable of reversing anticoagulant-related bleeding

Anticoagulant medications significantly increase the risk and severity of internal hemorrhage, including slow intracranial bleeding, even after relatively minor trauma, and this risk may not be apparent immediately
Blood thinners have no effect on bleeding risk after trauma, since these medications only work at the microscopic clotting level and do not meaningfully change how much a patient bleeds after injury
Blood thinners only affect bleeding from surgical wounds, not trauma, since these medications are specifically formulated to interact with the controlled bleeding of a surgical incision

q: An elderly patient with a urinary tract infection presents with acute confusion as the primary complaint, with no fever reported and normal-appearing vital signs by report. Why is this presentation clinically important to recognize?
options: This presentation rules out any infectious cause, since a true infection presents with fever and other classic systemic signs in patients of any age

In elderly patients, infections (including UTIs) can present atypically with acute confusion/delirium as the primary or only obvious symptom, rather than classic infection signs, making this an important but easily overlooked cause of altered mental status
UTIs never cause any symptoms other than urinary complaints in any age group, since the infection is localized to the urinary tract and cannot produce symptoms affecting other body systems
Acute confusion in the elderly is most often dementia and does not need further evaluation, since progressive cognitive decline is the most common explanation for new confusion in older adults

q: An elderly patient reports feeling '20% weaker than usual' and has fallen twice in the past week, but denies chest pain, shortness of breath, or other specific complaints. Why should vague complaints like generalized weakness in an elderly patient warrant a thorough assessment?
options: Vague weakness complaints in the elderly are never clinically significant, since generalized weakness without a specific associated symptom rarely reflects a true underlying medical emergency in this older population

Vague or nonspecific complaints (like generalized weakness) can be the presenting symptom of serious underlying conditions (cardiac, infectious, metabolic, or neurologic) in older adults, so a thorough assessment is warranted rather than dismissing the complaint
Weakness in the elderly is always caused by simple dehydration and requires no other workup, since inadequate fluid intake is by far the most common cause of generalized weakness
This complaint should be attributed entirely to normal aging with no further evaluation needed at all, since gradual loss of strength and occasional falls are an expected part of growing older

q: A geriatric patient has a blood pressure of 150/90 mmHg, which you know is elevated by general standards, but a family member states this is actually lower than the patient's normal baseline of 180/100. How should this affect your clinical interpretation?
options: Baseline blood pressure history is irrelevant to interpreting a single current reading, since a vital sign should always be evaluated purely against standard population reference norms alone
The patient's reported baseline should be disregarded entirely, since family-reported history of chronic hypertension is generally less reliable than a directly measured reading obtained today

This relatively lower reading compared to the patient's known baseline could actually represent a significant, clinically relevant drop, and should be interpreted in the context of the patient's normal baseline rather than generic 'normal' ranges alone

The reading should be treated as fully normal since it fits general population reference ranges, meaning a value of 150/90 mmHg requires no additional interpretation in light of the patient's known history

q: You are assessing an elderly patient with significant kyphosis (curvature of the upper spine) who requires spinal motion restriction after a fall. What modification to standard immobilization technique is often necessary?
options: The patient should be left unpadded to allow the board to conform to the spine, since a rigid backboard will naturally flex and mold itself to the patient's curvature over time
Immobilization should be abandoned entirely in any patient with kyphosis, since the curvature makes it impossible to achieve any degree of effective spinal motion restriction
No modification is needed for the patient's spinal curvature, since standard immobilization technique and equipment are designed to accommodate any body shape without adjustment

Additional padding (such as under the head/shoulders or along the back) is often needed to accommodate the patient's natural spinal curvature and maintain a neutral, comfortable alignment rather than forcing a flat position

q: An elderly patient with dementia becomes agitated and combative during assessment, striking out at the EMT. What approach best balances patient care needs with safety and respect for the patient?
options: Refuse to treat the patient at all and leave the scene, since a combative patient who cannot cooperate with assessment cannot be safely or ethically managed by EMS
Immediately restrain the patient physically without attempting any other approach, since a combative dementia patient requires prompt physical control to keep the crew and patient safe

Attempt calming techniques (a calm voice, involving a familiar caregiver, reducing overstimulation) first, using the least restrictive means necessary, escalating to restraint only if there is a genuine safety threat and per protocol
Sedate the patient using medications the EMT carries for other purposes, since chemical calming will resolve the agitation faster and more reliably than any verbal approach

q: A geriatric patient with reduced skin elasticity and thinning skin sustains what appears to be a minor skin tear from adhesive tape removal during a prior medical visit. Why does this happen more often in elderly patients, and how should the EMT modify bandaging technique?
options: This only occurs due to a rare skin disease and is not a general aging change, since healthy elderly skin without an underlying dermatologic condition tolerates tape removal normally

Aging skin becomes thinner and more fragile with reduced elasticity, making it prone to tearing from adhesives; EMTs should use gentler adhesives/techniques (such as roller gauze instead of tape directly on skin) when possible
Tape should be applied more tightly in elderly patients to compensate for weaker skin, since firmer adhesion helps prevent the dressing from shifting against fragile tissue
Elderly skin is identical to younger skin, so no modification is needed, since the structural properties of skin do not meaningfully change as a normal part of the aging process

q: You suspect elder abuse based on inconsistent injury explanations and evidence of neglect (poor hygiene, malnutrition) in a geriatric patient living with a caregiver. What is the appropriate EMT action?
options: Objectively document findings, report suspicions through appropriate channels (such as adult protective services or law enforcement, per local mandatory reporting requirements), and prioritize the patient's immediate medical needs and safety

Confront the caregiver directly and openly accuse them of abuse right on scene, since immediately addressing the suspected mistreatment gives the caregiver a fair chance to explain or correct the situation
Ignore the findings entirely since it is not the EMT's place to get involved, as investigating suspected abuse or neglect falls entirely outside EMT scope and responsibility
Refuse transport until the caregiver satisfactorily explains the situation to you, since withholding needed care from the patient creates useful leverage to obtain a truthful account

q: An elderly patient taking multiple medications (polypharmacy) presents with acute confusion and lethargy. Why is medication review especially important in this population when assessing altered mental status?
options: Only illegal drug use should be considered as a cause of altered mental status, since prescribed medications are regulated and therefore cannot be responsible for confusion or lethargy
Polypharmacy increases the risk of drug interactions, cumulative side effects, and dosing errors, any of which can cause altered mental status and should be considered alongside other causes
Medication lists are not useful information for EMS to gather, since determining the cause of altered mental status is entirely the responsibility of hospital staff, not EMS
Medications never interact with each other or cause altered mental status, since prescription drugs are formulated to act only on their intended target without broader cognitive effects

q: An elderly patient with limited mobility has developed a stage 3 pressure ulcer (through the skin into subcutaneous tissue) on the sacrum, discovered incidentally during assessment for an unrelated complaint. What should the EMT do regarding this finding?
options: Document the finding objectively and report it as part of the handoff, since it may indicate a need for further evaluation, wound care, or a review of home care adequacy
Refuse to transport until the wound is addressed on scene, since a pressure ulcer of this severity should not be left untreated any longer than absolutely necessary
Ignore it completely since it is unrelated to the chief complaint, as findings that do not connect to why EMS was called do not need to be mentioned or documented in the report
Attempt to debride or treat the wound in the field, since removing damaged tissue and dressing the ulcer now will speed the patient's recovery once they reach the hospital

q: A pregnant patient at approximately 32 weeks gestation is found supine after a fall and reports feeling dizzy and nauseated, with a drop in blood pressure noted. What is the most likely cause, and what simple intervention should be tried first?
options: Cardiogenic shock; the patient should remain supine with her legs elevated to improve venous return to a heart that is struggling to pump effectively on its own
An allergic reaction requiring immediate epinephrine administration, since a sudden drop in blood pressure combined with nausea can be an early sign of a developing anaphylactic response
A normal finding in pregnancy requiring no positional change, since dizziness, nausea, and lower blood pressure while lying flat are common and harmless at this stage of gestation for most patients

Supine hypotensive syndrome from the gravid uterus compressing the inferior vena cava; positioning the patient on her left side (or manually displacing the uterus leftward if she must remain supine, such as on a backboard) should be tried

q: A pregnant patient in her third trimester presents with sudden, severe abdominal pain, dark vaginal bleeding, and a rigid, tender abdomen. What condition does this presentation most strongly suggest, and why is it dangerous for both mother and fetus?
options: Normal labor contractions, which can cause similar discomfort but do not produce a rigid, board-like abdomen or dark vaginal bleeding, so only standard transport and monitoring are needed
Placenta previa, in which the placenta covers the cervix and typically presents with a rigid, board-like abdomen along with severe pain
Braxton Hicks contractions, painless practice contractions that do not cause bleeding, abdominal rigidity, or any urgent need for transport
Placental abruption, in which the placenta separates prematurely from the uterine wall, risking severe maternal hemorrhage and cutting off the fetal oxygen/nutrient supply

q: During a field delivery, the umbilical cord is found prolapsed (visible at the vaginal opening ahead of the presenting fetal part). What is the priority EMT action?
options: Attempt to manually push the prolapsed cord back up into the vaginal canal past the presenting fetal part, believing this restores normal fetal circulation and directly relieves compression on the cord
Pull firmly on the exposed cord to hasten delivery of the fetus, since completing the birth quickly would relieve the cord compression

Position the mother in a knee-chest or Trendelenburg-type position, apply gentle upward pressure on the presenting fetal part with a gloved hand to relieve cord compression, keep the cord moist, and transport emergently without removing the hand
Clamp and cut the umbilical cord immediately before delivery is complete, in order to stop the presenting part from compressing it further

q: A newly delivered newborn is limp, cyanotic, and has a heart rate of 80 beats per minute after initial drying and stimulation. What is the priority intervention?
options: Begin positive-pressure ventilation with a BVM, since a newborn heart rate below 100/min despite initial stimulation indicates inadequate response and the need for assisted ventilation
Withhold all intervention and simply monitor for several minutes, since a limp, cyanotic newborn with a heart rate of 80/min often self-corrects without any assisted breathing
Begin chest compressions immediately without attempting ventilation first, since a heart rate of 80/min after stimulation already meets the threshold for starting compressions
Continue drying and stimulating only, since a heart rate of 80/min is considered close enough to normal that assisted ventilation is not yet warranted at this stage

q: A mother has just delivered a healthy newborn in the field, and delivery of the placenta has not yet occurred when you note significant, ongoing vaginal bleeding. What is the appropriate management?
options: Delay transport until the placenta has fully delivered on its own, since transporting before delivery is complete is thought to risk further injury
Pull firmly on the umbilical cord to hasten placental delivery, since removing the placenta quickly may help control the ongoing hemorrhage
Pack the vaginal canal tightly with rolled gauze in order to directly tamponade and control the source of the bleeding on scene before continuing on with transport

Massage the fundus of the uterus (once delivered, or as appropriate per protocol) to encourage contraction, allow the placenta to deliver on its own, and manage ongoing hemorrhage with standard shock precautions while transporting

q: A pregnant patient at 38 weeks presents with a blood pressure of 168/108, severe headache, visual disturbances, and swelling of her hands and face. What condition is most concerning, and what serious complication should the EMT anticipate and prepare for?
options: Gestational diabetes, since swelling and headache are viewed as common associated symptoms, making an oral glucose check the priority intervention
Normal blood pressure changes expected in the third trimester, since pressure often rises somewhat late in pregnancy and this particular reading requires no specific action
Preeclampsia, with risk of progression to eclampsia (seizures)
Simple pregnancy-related fatigue, since headache and swelling are considered common, unremarkable complaints in the third trimester that do not require further evaluation

q: A woman in labor reports a strong urge to push and crowning is visible on exam, but you are still 25 minutes from the hospital by transport time. What is the correct course of action?
options: Delay delivery by having the mother cross her legs tightly and rushing emergently to the hospital, on the reasoning that crowning does not necessarily mean birth is truly imminent
Attempt to physically delay the birth by applying firm pressure to hold the fetal head back until arrival at the hospital
Refuse to assist delivery under any circumstances and wait for ALS backup no matter the timeline, on the reasoning that field delivery falls outside EMT-B scope of practice
Prepare to assist with an imminent field delivery, since crowning indicates delivery is imminent and there generally is not time to safely reach the hospital first

q: A newborn is delivered with meconium-stained (greenish) amniotic fluid, and the baby is vigorous, crying, with good muscle tone immediately after birth. What is the current recommended approach to airway management in this specific scenario?
options: Since the baby is vigorous, provide routine care (drying, warming, and clearing the mouth/nose as needed) rather than performing routine tracheal suctioning, per current neonatal resuscitation guidance
Immediately intubate and perform tracheal suctioning below the vocal cords regardless of the baby's vigor, since any meconium exposure is treated as requiring this invasive airway clearing
Withhold all care and drying because meconium exposure means the baby should not be touched until dedicated suctioning equipment is fully ready
Immediately submerge the newborn in water to dilute and rinse away the meconium before performing any other assessment or care

q: A patient reports she is pregnant and has vaginal bleeding without pain in her third trimester, with bright red blood and no abdominal rigidity. What condition should be suspected, and how should the EMT approach the pelvic exam?
options: Ectopic pregnancy, which can occur later in pregnancy and would explain painless bright red vaginal bleeding at this stage
Normal spotting in pregnancy requiring no special precaution, since bright red bleeding without pain is treated as a common, unremarkable third-trimester finding
Placental abruption; perform a digital vaginal exam to assess cervical dilation and determine how far labor has already progressed
Possible placenta previa; a digital vaginal or internal exam should be avoided in the field, since it can provoke severe hemorrhage if the placenta is covering the cervix

q: An infant presents with lethargy, a sunken fontanelle, dry mucous membranes, and decreased urine output per the caregiver, following several days of vomiting and diarrhea. What condition does this suggest, and why is it especially dangerous in infants?
options: Normal findings in a healthy, well-hydrated infant, since lethargy and decreased urine output are treated as expected after a viral illness with vomiting and diarrhea
Significant dehydration, which can progress to hypovolemic shock quickly in infants due to their smaller fluid reserves and higher relative fluid losses
A benign viral illness requiring no assessment of hydration status, since vomiting and diarrhea in infants are assumed to resolve without specific monitoring
A sign of overhydration from excessive fluid intake during the illness, which would call for fluid restriction rather than any replacement therapy

q: A 4-year-old with a high fever is brought to you seizing for the first time, with no prior seizure history. The seizure resolves spontaneously after about 90 seconds. What is this presentation most consistent with, and how should it be managed?
options: A sign of meningitis in all cases, requiring immediate antibiotic administration by the EMT to treat the presumed underlying infection
A breath-holding spell requiring no further action or transport, since these episodes are typically brief, self-limited, and unrelated to fever
Epilepsy requiring the EMT to make long-term anticonvulsant therapy decisions in the field, since a seizure with fever is treated as proof of an underlying seizure disorder

A likely febrile seizure; supportive care (protecting the airway, positioning, managing the fever per protocol) and transport for evaluation are appropriate, even though the seizure has already resolved

q: An infant is found unresponsive, not breathing, with no pulse. On exam, you note lividity (pooling of blood) and rigor in the extremities, and the caregiver reports the infant was last checked several hours ago. What does this finding indicate, and how should it change resuscitation efforts?
options: These findings mean the infant should be transported emergently with lights and sirens running so that full resuscitation can continue en route and at the receiving hospital
These are early, potentially reversible findings consistent with a very recent arrest, so full resuscitation should still be attempted regardless of how long the infant was last checked
Only rigor mortis actually indicates true death; lividity alone is considered a reversible finding that still requires full resuscitation efforts to be attempted

Lividity and rigor are obvious signs of death; per most protocols, resuscitation is not initiated in the presence of these clear, irreversible signs, though local protocols and family support/communication remain important

q: A 2-year-old chokes on a piece of food and is now unable to cry, cough, or make any sound, with visible cyanosis developing. What is the correct sequence of maneuvers for this age group?
options: Blind finger sweeps of the airway performed as the very first step taken, in order to physically locate and remove the obstructing object before attempting any other maneuver
Abdominal thrusts (Heimlich maneuver) only, performed exactly as they would be done in an adult, since the technique for clearing a foreign body airway obstruction is the same at every age
No physical intervention should be attempted; wait for the child to dislodge the object independently, since forceful maneuvers can injure young children

Alternating back blows and chest thrusts, since abdominal thrusts are avoided in infants and generally cautioned against or modified in very young children due to organ injury risk (with local protocol determining the exact pediatric age cutoff)

q: A school-age child with a history of asthma presents with severe respiratory distress, is unable to speak, has a silent chest, and is becoming drowsy. Compared to a milder asthma exacerbation, what does drowsiness in this context indicate?
options: An unrelated finding, likely just simple tiredness from crying and struggling earlier during this episode, with no real bearing on the child's current respiratory status
A normal, expected response to the albuterol treatment already given, since bronchodilators like albuterol commonly cause temporary drowsiness as breathing eases
Improvement, since the child appears calmer and noticeably less agitated than before, suggesting the underlying airway distress and bronchospasm are beginning to resolve on their own

A dangerous sign of hypoxia and impending respiratory failure, since increasing lethargy/drowsiness in a child with severe respiratory distress often indicates the child is tiring and beginning to fail, not improving

q: A 6-month-old infant presents with a fever, is unusually irritable with a high-pitched cry, and has a bulging fontanelle. What serious condition should be strongly suspected, and what physical exam finding should be handled especially gently?
options: Possible meningitis; the bulging fontanelle reflects increased intracranial pressure and should be noted (not pressed on forcefully) as part of a gentle exam, with rapid transport prioritized
A dental teething issue causing the fever and irritability, requiring no further workup since teething commonly causes fever and irritability in infants this age
A simple viral cold; the fontanelle finding is treated as a normal variant requiring no further concern or workup
Dehydration; a bulging fontanelle is often seen with significant fluid loss in infants

q: A toddler presents with several bruises in different stages of healing on the back and buttocks (areas not typically injured by normal childhood activity), along with a caregiver's story that doesn't match the pattern of injury. What should the EMT do?
options: Refuse to transport the child at all until the caregiver provides a fully satisfactory explanation for the observed pattern and history of the bruising found

Recognize this pattern as concerning for possible non-accidental trauma (child abuse), document objectively, treat the child's medical needs, and report through appropriate channels per mandatory reporting laws
Ignore the finding entirely, since toddlers commonly bruise from normal play and falls, even in less typical locations like the back and buttocks
Confront the caregiver directly on scene and accuse them of causing the bruising, in order to immediately address the suspected abuse

q: You are ventilating an infant with a BVM and notice the chest is rising excessively with each breath, more than the gentle rise expected. What risk does this create, and how should technique be adjusted?
options: The mask should be removed and mouth-to-mouth ventilation used instead, since this method makes it easier to control the volume of air delivered
The current technique should remain unchanged, since infants require proportionally larger tidal volumes per breath relative to body size than adults do

Risk of barotrauma (lung injury) and gastric distension leading to aspiration; ventilations should be gentler, using just enough volume to produce a visible, gentle chest rise, appropriate to the infant's smaller lung volume
A larger, more visible chest rise indicates more effective ventilation and better oxygen delivery in infants than a subtle rise would, so no adjustment is needed

q: A 7-year-old with a fever and sore throat is sitting in the 'sniffing position,' drooling, refusing to lie down, and has a muffled voice. The caregiver reports rapid onset over just a few hours, and the child has not received the Hib vaccine. What condition should be strongly suspected, and how should the exam proceed?
options: Strep throat, which commonly causes drooling and voice changes in children this age; have the child gargle salt water and take oral fluids before transport begins
Croup, which typically requires prompt intubation by EMS to secure the airway before transport

Possible epiglottitis; avoid agitating the child, including examining the throat with a tongue depressor or forcing positioning changes, and transport promptly allowing the child to remain in the position of comfort
A simple cold; a thorough oral exam using a tongue depressor should be performed on the child to confirm this diagnosis before proceeding with transport to the hospital

q: At a multi-agency incident, you notice that both fire and EMS command are giving conflicting instructions to responders on scene. What structural element of the Incident Command System is likely missing or not being followed?
options: The National Incident Management System, which applies mainly to federally declared disasters rather than routine multi-agency responses
Unified command, which allows multiple agencies to coordinate through a single, integrated command structure with agreed-upon objectives
A rehabilitation (rehab) sector, which is unrelated to command conflicts and instead addresses responder rest and hydration needs
The use of radios, which should be replaced with in-person communication only, since verbal relay between crews resolves most conflicting orders

q: During a mass-casualty incident, you are assigned as a triage officer under ICS. To whom should you report your triage counts and updates?
options: Directly to incident command, bypassing any intermediate supervisors, since command needs every detail firsthand to make decisions
Directly to the hospital emergency department charge nurse, bypassing the on-scene ICS structure entirely to save time
To local media to keep the public informed of the ongoing triage counts and casualty updates
To your immediate supervisor within the ICS structure (such as a medical branch/group supervisor), maintaining the chain of command rather than bypassing it

q: You are providing a radio report to the receiving hospital for a critical trauma patient. Which format best ensures the report is clear, organized, and complete?
options: A stream-of-consciousness narrative covering whatever assessment details come to mind first for the crew, without any particular order, structure, or format applied
A structured format (such as unit ID/ETA, patient age/sex, chief complaint, pertinent history, vital signs, treatment given, and response to treatment) delivered concisely
A report focused exclusively on describing the mechanism of injury in detail, while deliberately omitting any vital signs or treatment information from the transmission entirely
Only the patient's name and a requested room number upon arrival, without providing any clinical details at all about the patient's condition, vitals, or treatment

q: During a large-scale incident, cellular and radio communications become overloaded and unreliable. What backup communication strategy is most appropriate for maintaining coordination between units?
options: Abandon any attempt at coordinated communication entirely and operate independently until normal channels happen to be restored on their own at some point
Wait indefinitely on scene for normal communications to be fully restored before taking any further action, decision, or resource request whatsoever
Rely solely on personal cell phones to text incident command directly, since cell networks typically remain reliable even during large-scale incidents
Use predetermined backup methods (such as runners, established rally points, or alternate radio channels/frequencies per the incident communications plan) to maintain coordination

q: You are the first EMS unit to arrive at a large, complex incident with multiple patients and hazards. Before treating any patient, what should be your first action regarding incident command?
options: Begin transporting patients individually as each one is found, with no overall size-up performed at all and no organized triage system applied to the scene
Wait for a chief officer to physically arrive before taking any action, since only a chief officer has the authority to establish initial command
Immediately begin treating the most visibly injured patient found first, without broadcasting any size-up report or organizing the overall scene beforehand at all
Establish or report to incident command (or transfer command appropriately) and provide an initial size-up report to incoming units, since your first actions set the framework for the entire response

q: At a hazardous materials incident, you are assigned to work in the 'warm zone' rehab area. What is the primary purpose of this ICS functional area?
options: To store equipment that is entirely unrelated to patient care, kept separate from any responder rest, hydration, or medical monitoring function nearby
To serve as the primary incident command post from which all responding agencies coordinate operations at the ongoing hazardous materials incident
To provide definitive decontamination of contaminated patients before they are allowed to move any deeper into the warm zone toward the treatment sector itself
To monitor and support responder health and safety (rest, hydration, vital sign checks) during extended operations, reducing risk of responder injury or illness

q: You are handing off a patient to a flight crew for air medical transport at a rural scene. What is a key safety consideration specific to helicopter operations that ground EMS must follow?
options: There are no special safety considerations different from ground ambulance operations when working around a landed helicopter
Approaching the aircraft while it is still landing, to save time before the rotors fully settle
Approaching only from the front or sides within the pilot's clear view, never near the tail rotor, and only when signaled by flight crew that it is safe to approach
Approaching the helicopter from the rear, near the tail rotor, since this offers the fastest, most direct approach to the aircraft

q: During interfacility transport, you receive a detailed handoff report from the sending facility nurse but notice a discrepancy between the reported medication dose and what is documented on the paperwork. What should you do?
options: Ignore both the verbal report and the paperwork, and administer a different dose based on your own independent protocol
Guess which one is correct and use your own judgment silently, without raising the discrepancy with sending staff
Clarify the discrepancy directly with the sending facility staff before departing, to ensure an accurate understanding of the patient's actual treatment
Proceed with the documented dose without clarifying the discrepancy, since the written paperwork is generally the more reliable source

q: You are dispatched to a scene already being managed by a fire department using ICS, and you are the ranking EMS officer arriving. What should your first action be regarding the command structure already in place?
options: Ignore the existing ICS structure entirely and direct EMS operations independently of the fire department's command
Immediately establish a separate, independent EMS command structure alongside the fire department's existing command
Report to the established incident commander (or transfer to a unified command structure if appropriate) rather than creating a separate, uncoordinated command
Take command from the fire department immediately, since medical care is the primary need and EMS should direct the overall response

q: A mutual aid ambulance from a neighboring jurisdiction arrives to assist at a large incident but uses different terminology and slightly different triage tag colors than your local system. What ICS principle is designed to help address this kind of interoperability challenge?
options: Only the mutual aid unit's own agency leadership should be permitted to make decisions for that crew, operating fully independently of local incident command for the entire incident

Common terminology and standardized procedures (a core ICS principle) are designed to reduce confusion between agencies, and incident command should quickly brief incoming mutual aid units on any local variations
Mutual aid units should be sent back home upon arrival if their terminology or equipment differs from the local system, since integrating them safely under those conditions is difficult
Mutual aid units should not be integrated into ongoing operations when their terminology or equipment differs from the local system

q: A competent adult patient with a life-threatening condition refuses transport after being informed of the risks, including possible death. The EMT believes this decision is unwise. What is the legally and ethically correct action?
options: Call the patient's family to override the patient's own decision, treating family consent as superior to the competent patient's own wishes
Transport the patient against their will, since a life-threatening condition overrides the patient's right to refuse
Respect the patient's right to refuse care and transport as long as they have decision-making capacity, have been informed of the risks, and the refusal is properly documented
Sedate the patient to allow transport despite the refusal, since sedating her resolves the conflict between ensuring safety and respecting her wishes

q: You are treating a 16-year-old patient with a significant injury, and the patient's parents cannot be reached. Under the doctrine EMS typically relies on in this situation, how should you proceed?
options: Require the minor to sign their own legal consent form before treatment, since a 16-year-old is generally considered old enough to independently authorize their own care
Withhold all treatment until a parent or guardian can be contacted, since treatment generally requires direct parental consent before it can begin
Provide necessary emergency treatment under implied consent, since a reasonable parent would want necessary care for their injured/ill child, and continue attempting to reach a parent
Call law enforcement to make all medical decisions for the minor, since officers are considered to hold authority over treatment choices in this situation

q: An EMT documents a patient assessment finding that was not actually performed, in order to make the patient care report appear more complete. What is this practice called, and why is it a serious concern?
options: Standard, generally acceptable practice within busy EMS systems, since a plausible-looking finding fills documentation gaps without causing real harm
Acceptable as long as the patient's ultimate outcome happened to be good, since a favorable outcome justifies the inaccurate documentation entry after the fact
A minor administrative shortcut carrying no real consequence, since the PCR is often treated as a paperwork formality rather than a genuine clinical or legal document

Falsification of records, which is both an ethical violation and potentially illegal, since it creates inaccurate medical/legal records that can harm patient care and expose the EMT and agency to serious liability

q: A bystander who is a physician arrives on scene and begins directing care that conflicts with your protocols, without any documented relationship with your EMS system or medical direction. How should the EMT handle this situation?
options: Ignore the bystander physician completely and refuse any interaction with them at all, since an unaffiliated bystander physician has no real authority or useful role in this situation

Politely explain that you operate under your service's medical direction and protocols, and generally continue to follow those unless the bystander physician is willing to take over care, accompany the patient to the hospital, and accept documented responsibility per local protocol
Immediately abandon your own established protocols in order to fully comply with the bystander's instructions, since a physician's direction on scene supersedes the EMT's own protocols
Always defer entirely to any physician present on scene, since any active medical license outranks established EMS protocol

q: An unconscious patient is found with a medical alert bracelet indicating a specific allergy and chronic condition. Is the EMT legally permitted to act on this information without the patient's ability to verbally consent?
options: Only law enforcement can authorize use of a medical alert bracelet's information, since interpreting it falls outside EMS authority
The information should be ignored since it cannot be verified in the field, and information that cannot be verified should not be used to guide treatment decisions
No, all care must stop until verbal consent is obtained, since implied consent does not apply to an unresponsive adult patient who cannot verbally agree
Yes, this falls under implied consent for emergency care, and the medical alert information should be used to inform appropriate treatment decisions

q: You witness a fellow EMT perform a skill incorrectly in a way that could have harmed the patient, though the patient appears to be unaffected in the immediate term. What is the most appropriate ethical action?
options: Say nothing to the coworker or anyone else in order to avoid conflict, since the patient appearing currently unaffected removes any need to report the error
Alter your own documentation of the call in order to quietly cover for the coworker's error, since this protects the coworker without further harming the patient

Address the concern through appropriate channels (such as directly with the coworker if appropriate, and/or reporting to a supervisor/quality improvement process), and ensure any necessary follow-up care or documentation occurs for the patient
Publicly confront the coworker in front of the patient and family right at the scene, since immediate correction ensures accountability

q: A patient with capacity refuses a specific intervention (such as an IV) but consents to transport and other care. How should the EMT proceed?
options: Perform the refused IV anyway since transport itself was agreed to, since consenting to transport implies consent to every other proposed intervention as well
Consider the patient's entire consent invalid because of this one partial refusal, treating any single declined intervention as voiding all of the other agreed-upon care

Respect the patient's right to selectively refuse specific interventions while consenting to others, documenting the specific refusal, and proceed with the care and transport the patient has agreed to
Refuse to transport the patient at all unless she consents to every single proposed intervention, treating informed consent as a strict all-or-nothing package deal

q: During transport, a patient's condition changes such that continuing to a further, specialized facility (per protocol) versus a closer general hospital becomes a judgment call, and the patient's family is pressuring you to go to the closer facility against your protocol-based destination decision. What should guide your decision?
options: Always defer to the family's stated wishes over your protocol-based destination criteria, since family preference should outweigh established transport protocols when they disagree
Refuse to communicate with the family about the decision at all, since explaining the protocol-based reasoning to them would only add to their distress
Go with whichever facility the family requests when both options seem reasonable, since their preference and protocol carry similar weight in this kind of judgment call

Follow your protocol-based destination criteria (such as stroke or trauma center criteria) and, if needed, consult medical direction, while communicating clearly and compassionately with the family about the reasoning

q: You respond to a call and recognize the patient as a coworker's family member with a sensitive medical/psychiatric condition. What ethical obligation applies regarding patient confidentiality in this situation?
options: The same patient confidentiality obligations (such as those under HIPAA and general EMS ethics) apply regardless of any personal relationship, and the EMT should avoid discussing the patient's condition with others, including the coworker, without proper authorization
Confidentiality does not apply to personal acquaintances like this coworker, since a known personal relationship removes the usual legal protections
Confidentiality can be verbally waived by the EMT alone without the patient's own consent, since the treating provider has sole discretion over disclosure decisions

It is acceptable to discuss the case details freely with the coworker since they are considered 'part of the EMS family,' and being part of the same EMS organization is generally accepted as sufficient authorization to share those details

q: You are called to a scene for a psychiatric emergency where the patient is reportedly armed with a knife. Law enforcement has not yet secured the scene. What is the correct action?
options: Approach cautiously with a taser or improvised weapon of your own for protection
Enter and attempt verbal de-escalation immediately since the patient needs help
Stage at a safe distance until law enforcement confirms the scene is secure and the weapon is controlled
Send one crew member in alone while the other stays at a safe distance

q: While extricating a patient from a vehicle with a partially deployed side-curtain airbag that has not fully discharged, what safety precaution should the crew take?
options: Manually trigger the airbag to deploy first in order to eliminate the risk before continuing, since intentionally triggering it under controlled conditions is safer than leaving it live

Treat the undeployed airbag as a hazard capable of still deploying, and take precautions (such as disconnecting the battery per protocol and keeping personnel clear of the airbag's deployment path) before extrication
Remove the entire airbag module using hand tools before beginning extrication, since physically detaching the module fully eliminates the underlying hazard
Ignore the airbag's status entirely and proceed with extrication as normal, since a partially deployed airbag has already released all of its stored energy

q: You arrive at a scene where a patient is in obvious distress inside a structure that has active fire showing from a window, with no fire department on scene yet. What is the correct EMT action?
options: Enter the structure immediately to rescue the patient since time is critical, since delaying rescue poses a greater risk to the patient than the active fire does
Stage at a safe distance and wait for fire department resources trained and equipped for structural firefighting/rescue, providing medical care once the patient is brought to a safe area
Enter without any protective equipment since delay could be fatal to the patient, since speed matters more than having the proper protective gear in this situation
Attempt to fight the fire yourself with an ambulance-mounted extinguisher before rescuing the patient, since a quick knockdown can clear a safe path inside

q: During a violent weather event, you are dispatched to a reported injury in an area under an active tornado warning. What should guide your response and on-scene operations?
options: Coordinate with dispatch/incident command regarding timing of response, prioritize personal and crew safety (seeking appropriate shelter if a tornado is imminent), and proceed with patient care once conditions allow safe operations
Ignore all weather-related guidance entirely since patient care takes precedence, and crew safety concerns can be addressed afterward
Refuse to respond to the call at all during an active tornado warning, since the entire warning area should be treated as equally unsafe throughout
Respond immediately and begin patient care regardless of the ongoing severe weather conditions, since the patient's needs outweigh the ongoing storm danger

q: You respond to a residence with several aggressive, unrestrained dogs visible in the yard as you approach, and the patient is located inside the home. What is the correct approach?
options: Attempt to befriend or feed the dogs before entering, since offering food or acting calm will prevent an attack
Request that the dogs be secured (by the resident, animal control, or law enforcement if needed) before entering, prioritizing crew safety
Enter quickly, hoping the dogs will not notice, since moving quickly minimizes the chance of provoking them
Use physical force against the dogs to clear a path inside, since this is the fastest way to reach the patient

q: At a scene involving a suspected clandestine drug lab (evidenced by unusual chemical smells and improvised lab equipment visible through a window), what is the correct EMS action upon recognizing these signs?
options: Open windows and doors to ventilate the structure yourself before entering, so the fumes dissipate enough for safe patient access
Enter the structure to retrieve the patient quickly, since drug lab chemical hazards are typically minor and unlikely to cause serious harm to EMS crews
Withdraw to a safe distance immediately, treat this as a hazardous materials scene, and request appropriately trained and equipped resources (hazmat, law enforcement) before further action
Attempt to collect samples of the chemicals for identification so responding hazmat crews know what they are dealing with

q: You are operating at a highway incident and need to move your ambulance to a safer position. What is a key operational principle regarding ambulance placement at roadway scenes?
options: Park the ambulance directly at the scene facing oncoming traffic, since this positioning allows the fastest possible departure once the patient is loaded aboard

Position the ambulance to help block/protect the work area from traffic (often up-traffic or angled appropriately, per local protocol) while ensuring a safe path for departure and using appropriate warning devices (cones, flares, lighting)
Ambulance placement has little real bearing on scene safety at roadway incidents, since drivers are responsible for avoiding the scene regardless of parking
Always park as far from the scene as space allows, since distance alone is what keeps responders safe from oncoming traffic

q: While responding emergency traffic (lights and sirens) to a call, you approach a red light with heavy cross traffic. What is the correct practice regarding intersections during an emergency response?
options: Proceed through the intersection at normal speed without slowing, since lights and sirens grant the right of way over cross traffic
Increase speed through intersections to minimize the time spent in the danger zone where cross traffic could strike the vehicle
Slow down, ensure other traffic has yielded/stopped, and proceed through the intersection only when it is safe to do so, since lights and sirens request the right of way but do not guarantee it
Turn off sirens at intersections to avoid startling other drivers, since a quieter approach reduces the chance of a panicked or unpredictable reaction

q: You arrive at a scene involving downed trees and utility lines after a storm, with a patient trapped nearby. Which action best reflects appropriate scene size-up and safety practice?
options: Have the trapped patient attempt to move themselves away from the wire on their own before you make any contact with them or assess the surrounding scene
Use a wooden tree branch or similar improvised tool to personally move the downed wire aside, since wood does not conduct electricity, even when wet
Assume that any wire not currently and visibly sparking or arcing is safe enough to move aside or step over on the direct way toward the trapped patient nearby

Treat all downed wires as energized and dangerous until the utility company confirms otherwise, maintaining a safe perimeter and awaiting appropriate resources before approaching the patient if wires are near

q: A patient involved in a fall from standing height is found alert, but you notice unequal chest rise with each breath and use of accessory muscles, though the patient denies any breathing difficulty. What should guide your primary assessment interpretation?
options: Rely solely on the patient's own verbal denial of breathing difficulty and move on directly to the next assessment step without any further scrutiny of the exam finding
Delay assessing the patient's breathing any further, since the fact that he remains alert and speaking suggests his ventilation is currently adequate
Assume the unequal chest rise observed is simply a normal anatomical variant unique to this particular patient and therefore not worth any further investigation right now

Trust the objective findings (unequal chest rise, accessory muscle use) over the patient's subjective denial, since objective signs of inadequate breathing can be present even when a patient underreports symptoms

q: You are assisting ventilations on an obese patient and struggle to maintain an adequate BVM mask seal using a one-handed technique. What is the most effective correction?
options: Switch to a two-rescuer BVM technique, with one provider maintaining the mask seal with both hands while the second squeezes the bag
Give up on BVM ventilation entirely and switch to a nonrebreather mask instead, even though the patient's breathing remains inadequate
Use a smaller mask than indicated for the patient's face, since a smaller mask is easier to seal completely against the face
Increase the oxygen flow rate to the bag to compensate for the poor mask seal and leaking air

q: A patient with a suspected pneumothorax after blunt trauma has an SpO2 of 91% on a nonrebreather mask at 15 L/min, with increasing work of breathing. What should this trend suggest about the adequacy of the current oxygen delivery method?
options: The current oxygen delivery method is fully adequate as-is, and no change in monitoring, escalation, or intervention is needed despite the low SpO2 and the rising work of breathing observed
The trend suggests the underlying problem (developing pneumothorax) may be progressing beyond what passive oxygen alone can correct
The nonrebreather mask currently in use should be replaced with a nasal cannula, since a lower-flow device may be better tolerated given his ongoing distress
The SpO2 reading itself should be disregarded entirely as inaccurate in this patient, since pulse oximetry is often unreliable in trauma patients like this one

q: A patient with COPD and long-standing barrel chest deformity presents with acute worsening dyspnea, and you are unable to clearly assess for a pneumothorax by chest rise alone due to the chronic deformity. What should guide your assessment in this case?
options: Skip any further respiratory assessment entirely, since the barrel chest deformity makes any meaningful evaluation of this patient's breathing impossible
Assume that no pneumothorax is possible in patients with COPD, since their lungs are already so chronically diseased that a further acute lung injury like pneumothorax essentially cannot occur
Chest rise alone should always remain the sole determinant used to assess for a pneumothorax, regardless of the patient's known baseline chest wall anatomy or overall shape

Rely on a combination of findings — auscultation for symmetry of breath sounds, SpO2, mental status, and the patient's reported baseline — rather than chest rise alone, given the altered baseline anatomy

q: A patient in cardiac arrest is being ventilated with a BVM while compressions continue without an advanced airway in place. What is the correct approach to timing ventilations relative to compressions in adult two-rescuer CPR without an advanced airway?
options: Deliver one breath for every 5 compressions on a continuous, uninterrupted cycle throughout the resuscitation
Ventilate only once every 2 minutes regardless of how many compressions have been delivered in between
Ventilate continuously with the BVM without any pause in chest compressions, delivering breaths whenever convenient
Pause compressions briefly to deliver 2 ventilations after every 30 compressions, per the standard 30:2 ratio without an advanced airway

q: A patient with new-onset facial droop and slurred speech has a blood glucose of 38 mg/dL. After treating the hypoglycemia, the facial droop and slurred speech fully resolve within minutes. What does this course suggest?
options: Hypoglycemia and focal stroke-like neurological symptoms are unrelated physiologic processes, so this rapid resolution was just a coincidence of timing
The neurological symptoms were likely a stroke mimic caused by hypoglycemia
The patient should not be transported at all since the neurological symptoms have already fully and completely resolved on their own right after the glucose was administered
The patient had a true ischemic stroke that happened to resolve spontaneously on its own within minutes, and since it resolved, this presentation requires no further workup

q: A patient has significant bleeding from a scalp laceration, which the patient reports has been bleeding heavily since the injury. How should the EMT approach direct pressure on a scalp wound, especially if there's a possible underlying skull fracture?
options: Apply direct pressure carefully, using a lighter touch or pressure around (rather than directly onto) the area if a skull fracture or depressed segment is suspected, to avoid pushing bone fragments into the brain
Apply a tourniquet snugly and circumferentially around the entire head to control the scalp bleeding, in a manner similar to how one would be applied to a limb injury
Apply firm, direct pressure straight onto the wound itself regardless of any suspected underlying skull fracture or depressed bone segment located beneath the laceration
Never attempt to control scalp bleeding of any kind at all, since scalp bleeding is not typically considered life-threatening in most patients

q: A patient with suspected traumatic brain injury has vomited once and is at risk for aspiration, but also has a suspected spinal injury requiring motion restriction. How should the EMT manage the airway in this situation?
options: Withhold spinal motion restriction entirely because of the vomiting risk present, since airway management cannot be safely combined with spinal precautions
Keep the patient strictly supine at all times regardless of any ongoing vomiting risk present, since spinal precautions take priority over airway concerns
Be prepared to log-roll the patient (maintaining spinal alignment) onto their side to clear the airway if vomiting recurs, since airway protection takes priority even with a spinal injury
Insert an oropharyngeal airway regardless of the patient's intact gag reflex, since an oropharyngeal airway will protect the airway from vomited contents

q: You are treating a combative patient with a significant head injury who is refusing spinal motion restriction and other necessary care, and his combativeness appears to be caused by the injury itself rather than by a separate, informed refusal. How should the EMT approach this situation?
options: Immediately abandon all further care since the patient is verbally refusing at this moment, treating this outburst as a valid and fully legally binding refusal of the necessary care

Recognize that altered mental status from the injury itself likely impairs the patient's decision-making capacity, meaning a true informed refusal cannot be given, and proceed with necessary care under implied consent while using the safest possible approach and appropriate additional resources (such as law enforcement) if needed
Wait indefinitely on scene for the patient to spontaneously calm down before providing any care at all, regardless of how his underlying head injury may already be worsening in the meantime
Restrain the patient physically using any means available without ever considering safety, proportionality, or whether a genuinely less restrictive option might be available and appropriate

q: A woman at approximately 20 weeks gestation presents with vaginal bleeding, cramping, and passage of tissue. What is the most likely process occurring, and what is the priority for EMS?
options: An indication for an immediate cesarean delivery to be performed by the EMT right there at the scene, given the described severity of the bleeding and tissue passage
A normal, entirely benign finding of pregnancy at this gestational age requiring no evaluation, monitoring, or transport whatsoever from the responding EMS crew on scene
Preterm labor requiring the EMT to administer a tocolytic medication on scene in an attempt to stop the ongoing uterine contractions before beginning transport

A likely miscarriage (spontaneous abortion); the priority is supportive care, monitoring for shock, providing emotional support, and transporting the patient along with any passed tissue for evaluation

q: A 3-year-old presents with sudden onset of stridor and drooling while playing with small toys, with no fever and a sudden onset over minutes rather than hours. How does this presentation help differentiate the likely cause from epiglottitis or croup?
options: It cannot be differentiated from an infectious cause in any meaningful way, so treatment approach and transport priority would stay the same either way

A sudden onset without fever, associated with playing with small objects, raises suspicion for a foreign body airway obstruction rather than an infectious cause like epiglottitis or croup, which typically have a more gradual onset over hours with fever
This presentation actually confirms epiglottitis outright, since epiglottitis often presents with a sudden onset over minutes and without fever
This presentation rules out any true airway problem entirely, since stridor occurring without fever is not clinically significant in a child this age

q: During a large search-and-rescue operation under ICS, you notice that the span of control for the operations section chief has grown to include 12 direct reports, well beyond the recommended range. What problem does this create, and what is the ICS solution?
options: The correct solution here is to eliminate the entire operations section outright and redistribute its assigned personnel among the other command sections instead entirely
No problem exists at all in this case, since span of control has no real limit as long as the supervisor is experienced and well trained
The correct solution here is to have all twelve direct reports communicate straight to incident command themselves instead of routing communications through the operations section chief
It overwhelms the supervisor; ICS adds branches, divisions or groups to restore a 3–7 span

q: An EMT is asked by a law enforcement officer to draw blood from a combative, non-consenting patient for a legal blood alcohol test unrelated to any medical treatment the patient needs. What is the appropriate response?
options: Perform the requested blood draw only once the patient eventually stops physically resisting, treating his eventual passive compliance as sufficient legal consent for the entire procedure
Comply immediately with the requested blood draw since a law enforcement officer directly asked for it, since a law enforcement officer's request carries authority over EMS actions on scene

Decline to perform a procedure that is a law enforcement evidentiary function rather than medical care, and clarify that EMS blood draws are for patient treatment and monitoring purposes, referring the officer to appropriate legal/medical processes for evidentiary draws
Refuse to have any further interaction with law enforcement personnel for the remainder of the entire shift because of this one uncomfortable evidentiary request

q: A trauma patient has a heart rate of 128, BP 108/94 (a narrowed pulse pressure), cool clammy skin, and delayed capillary refill of 4 seconds. Select the (3) findings below that are classic indicators of compensated (early) shock.
options: Slow, deep respirations
Heart rate of 128 bpm
Warm, flushed skin
Narrowed pulse pressure (108/94)
Delayed capillary refill of 4 seconds

q: Which (2) of the following are objective indicators of adequate perfusion in an alert patient?
options: Capillary refill under 2 seconds
Strong, regular radial pulse
Pale, mottled skin
Patient's self-report of 'feeling fine'

q: Arrange the following steps of the primary assessment in the correct order, from first to last.
options: Form a general impression
Assess breathing for rate and quality
Assess mental status using AVPU
Ensure scene safety and take BSI precautions
Assess airway patency

q: Arrange the components of the OPQRST history tool in the correct order in which they are typically asked.
options: Severity on a 1-10 scale
Region/radiation of the pain
Provocation/palliation — what makes it better or worse
Onset — what were you doing when it started
Time — how long has it lasted / has it changed

q: A patient with a severe closed head injury exhibits a breathing pattern of gradually increasing tidal volume followed by gradually decreasing tidal volume, with a period of apnea before the cycle repeats. This pattern is best described as:
options: Cheyne-Stokes respirations
Agonal respirations
Biot's (ataxic) respirations
Kussmaul respirations

q: A patient reports a headache described as 'the worst headache of my life,' with sudden onset and no prior history of migraines. This classic phrasing is most strongly associated with which underlying condition?
options: Cluster headache
Sinus congestion
Subarachnoid hemorrhage
Tension headache

q: An alert 82-year-old presents with new confusion that began this morning, a temperature of 101.8°F, and foul-smelling urine reported by family. What is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's altered mental status?
options: Normal age-related cognitive decline
A urinary tract infection progressing toward sepsis
Primary psychiatric decompensation
Medication non-compliance alone, unrelated to infection

q: A patient with chronic diabetes and a history of similar prior episodes presents with sudden confusion, diaphoresis, and tremors that resolved completely after receiving oral glucose. What most likely caused this presentation?
options: Alcohol withdrawal
Hypoglycemia
A transient ischemic attack
Acute psychosis

q: You are sizing up a patient found unresponsive at the bottom of a stairwell with an empty pill bottle nearby, shallow snoring respirations, and pinpoint pupils. Select the (2) findings that should raise the most immediate concern for opioid-related respiratory depression.
options: Pinpoint pupils
The patient's location at the bottom of a stairwell
An empty pill bottle found several feet away
Shallow, snoring respirations

q: Select the (2) findings below that would make insertion of an oropharyngeal airway (OPA) inappropriate in an unresponsive patient.
options: An intact gag reflex
Suspected traumatic injury to the mandible with loose teeth
Complete absence of any gag reflex
A patent, unobstructed airway with adequate spontaneous breathing

q: Arrange the following steps for performing a jaw-thrust maneuver on a trauma patient with a suspected spinal injury, in the correct order.
options: Place fingers behind the angles of the mandible bilaterally
Push the mandible forward without tilting the head or neck
Reassess airway patency and breathing after the maneuver
Position yourself at the top of the patient's head without moving the neck

q: A patient with a long-standing asthma history presents in severe distress, but you notice their wheezing — which had been loud — has now become nearly silent, while their work of breathing and anxiety appear to be worsening. What does this change most likely indicate?
options: A developing “silent chest” — airflow too poor to make sound, and failure is near
The stethoscope is malfunctioning and should be replaced before reassessing
The bronchospasm is resolving and the patient is improving
The patient has fully recovered normal lung sounds

q: A patient with a known history of heart failure presents with severe dyspnea, pink frothy sputum, and diffuse crackles (rales) heard bilaterally on auscultation. Which underlying process best explains this specific combination of findings?
options: Hyperventilation syndrome from anxiety
A simple, uncomplicated upper respiratory infection
Spontaneous pneumothorax
Acute pulmonary edema from left-sided heart failure

q: A patient with a history of COPD is found breathing through pursed lips and sitting upright leaning forward on his arms (tripod position), with a respiratory rate of 28. What is the most likely reason this patient has adopted this specific posture and breathing technique?
options: The patient is exhibiting early signs of a stroke affecting motor control of breathing
The patient is attempting to hide the severity of their breathing difficulty from the crew
These behaviors are self-taught compensatory mechanisms to keep airways open longer and maximize accessory muscle use during severe respiratory distress
The tripod position and pursed-lip breathing are involuntary reflexes with no functional benefit to the patient

q: A conscious patient with mild shortness of breath and an SpO2 of 95% on room air asks for oxygen. Based on current EMS guidance, what is the most appropriate initial approach to supplemental oxygen for this patient?
options: Apply oxygen only if the patient's SpO2 falls below 70%
Apply a nonrebreather at 15 L/min regardless of the patient's current oxygen saturation
Withhold all oxygen, since any supplemental oxygen is now considered universally harmful
Titrate oxygen delivery to maintain a normal SpO2, using the lowest concentration device needed rather than automatically maximizing flow

q: A patient in anaphylaxis develops audible stridor and increasing hoarseness of voice. What does this specific combination of findings most likely indicate?
options: An unrelated vocal cord injury from recent shouting
Progressive upper airway swelling that may rapidly lead to complete airway obstruction
Resolution of the allergic reaction as swelling subsides
A normal, expected side effect of epinephrine that requires no further concern

q: Select the (3) findings below that are classic warning signs of acute coronary syndrome (ACS) in a middle-aged patient.
options: Sharp, stabbing pain that worsens with a deep breath and palpation
Crushing substernal chest pressure radiating to the left arm or jaw
Diaphoresis with nausea
Pain that fully resolves within seconds when the patient changes position
Shortness of breath accompanying the chest discomfort

q: Select the (2) findings that together are most consistent with an opioid toxidrome.
options: Dilated (blown) pupils
Severely depressed respiratory rate
Pinpoint pupils
Hyperthermia and agitation

q: Arrange the following steps for assisting a patient with their own prescribed nitroglycerin, in the correct order.
options: Have the patient place the tablet or spray under the tongue
Confirm the medication has not expired and check for the characteristic burning/tingling sensation as a potency check
Confirm the patient has a physician-prescribed nitroglycerin and meets systolic BP criteria per protocol
Reassess blood pressure and pain level after administration

q: A patient describes intermittent leg pain that occurs reliably after walking a certain distance and resolves promptly with rest, without any pain at rest. This pattern is most consistent with which condition?
options: Deep vein thrombosis
A simple muscle cramp unrelated to circulation
Acute compartment syndrome
Intermittent claudication from peripheral arterial disease

q: A patient with type 1 diabetes presents with deep, rapid (Kussmaul) respirations, fruity-smelling breath, dry mucous membranes, and a blood glucose of 480 mg/dL. This presentation is most consistent with which condition?
options: A simple case of dehydration unrelated to blood glucose
Alcohol intoxication
Hypoglycemia
Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)

q: A patient with a known seizure disorder is found postictal — drowsy, confused, and slow to respond — several minutes after a witnessed generalized seizure ended. What is the most appropriate interpretation of this presentation?
options: This should be treated identically to a primary stroke, including immediate stroke-specific interventions
This confirms the patient is having a second, ongoing seizure right now that requires the same emergency intervention
This is an expected, self-limited postictal state that should be closely monitored while it resolves, rather than treated as a new independent emergency
This indicates the patient is faking their symptoms since a true seizure would not cause any lingering effects

q: Select the (3) steps below that are part of the correct, current sequence for managing severe external extremity hemorrhage.
options: Elevate the limb above the heart as the primary and only intervention needed
Apply a tourniquet immediately if direct pressure fails to control life-threatening bleeding
Apply direct pressure to the wound
Use a hemostatic dressing with pressure if direct pressure alone is inadequate and a tourniquet isn't yet indicated or available
Wait several minutes to see if bleeding slows on its own before intervening

q: Select the (2) findings that, when both present after blunt chest trauma, are most concerning for a developing tension pneumothorax.
options: Equal, clear breath sounds bilaterally
Tracheal deviation away from the affected side
Jugular venous distension with hypotension
A single, small area of bruising over the ribs with normal vital signs

q: Arrange the following steps of the rapid trauma assessment approach for a critically injured, altered patient in the correct order.
options: Begin transport and continue reassessment en route
Perform a rapid head-to-toe exam for life threats
Gather a focused history (SAMPLE) as time and patient condition allow
Obtain baseline vital signs
Complete the primary assessment (airway, breathing, circulation) and identify any immediate interventions

q: A patient involved in a high-speed motor vehicle collision has a rigid, distended abdomen with diffuse tenderness, along with tachycardia and a falling blood pressure, despite no visible external bleeding. What does this presentation most likely indicate?
options: A benign muscle strain from the seatbelt
A urinary tract infection unrelated to the collision
Simple gastric distension from swallowed air
Internal hemorrhage within the abdominal cavity

q: A patient with a lower leg injury reports pain that is disproportionate to the visible injury, worsened significantly by passive stretching of the toes, along with a tight, tense feeling in the calf. Distal pulses are still palpable. What condition should this presentation raise strong suspicion for?
options: Acute compartment syndrome
Peripheral neuropathy unrelated to the injury
Normal post-injury soreness
A simple ankle sprain

q: A trauma patient's blood pressure remains within normal limits despite an estimated significant blood loss, while their heart rate is markedly elevated. What does this combination most likely represent?
options: Definitive proof that no significant blood loss has actually occurred
Decompensated shock, since blood pressure is the only vital sign that matters
Compensated shock, where the body's mechanisms are still able to maintain blood pressure despite ongoing blood loss
A normal, expected finding requiring no further concern or monitoring

q: A patient sustains a partial-thickness burn covering an estimated 20% of their total body surface area, with blistering and intense pain. What does the presence of blistering and intense pain (rather than painless, leathery skin) tell you about the depth of this burn?
options: Burn depth cannot be estimated from pain level or blistering under any circumstances
It indicates a full-thickness (third-degree) burn with destroyed nerve endings
It indicates a superficial (first-degree) burn affecting only the outermost skin layer
It indicates a partial-thickness (second-degree) burn where nerve endings remain intact and viable

q: Select the (2) findings in a third-trimester pregnant patient that should raise immediate concern for preeclampsia.
options: Normal blood pressure with no other symptoms
A single episode of mild ankle swelling with normal blood pressure
Severe headache with visual disturbances
Significantly elevated blood pressure compared to her baseline

q: Select the (3) findings on the Pediatric Assessment Triangle (appearance, work of breathing, circulation to skin) that would indicate a child is seriously ill and needs urgent intervention.
options: Limp muscle tone and poor eye contact (abnormal appearance)
Pale or mottled skin color (abnormal circulation)
Playful, consolable, and making good eye contact
Pink skin color with brisk capillary refill
Visible retractions and nasal flaring (abnormal work of breathing)

q: Arrange the following steps for assisting an imminent, uncomplicated vaginal delivery in the field, in the correct order.
options: Dry, warm, and stimulate the newborn immediately after delivery
Support the head as it delivers, checking for a nuchal cord
Suction the mouth then the nose once the head is delivered
Deliver the shoulders by gently guiding the head downward then upward
Position the mother and prepare a clean delivery field

q: A 4-month-old presents with a history of poor feeding, lethargy, and a bulging fontanelle, with a caregiver whose account of how the infant was injured keeps changing and is inconsistent with the injuries observed. What should this combination of findings raise suspicion for?
options: Non-accidental trauma (abusive head trauma)
Simple viral gastroenteritis unrelated to trauma
Expected teething symptoms for this age
A normal variant of infant fontanelle development
